docs.title: Fauerbot Devlog
docs.text:
A software engineer (Python by trade, macOS by habit) and Claude rebuild an old dream, an autonomous lawnmower, entirely in simulation first.

The rules of the game:

  • Everything is code. Docker, bash, Makefiles, pinned versions. If it can't be rebuilt with one command, it doesn't count.
  • Telemetry first. Before a component gets code, it gets a telemetry contract: what will we want to know about it? Every run lands in Elasticsearch and shows up in Kibana.
  • The repo is the memory. Claude sessions die (usage limits, WSL restarts). PROGRESS.md and this blog are how we never lose the thread.

This blog is the story of what we built, what broke, and what we learned, with screenshots along the way.

Stack: ROS 2 Jazzy · Gazebo Harmonic · Nav2 · Elasticsearch & Kibana 9.5 · Docker on WSL2 · an RTX 4080 · MicroPython (eventually).

docs.title: A robot that lies about where it is
docs.text: Phase 2 put a mower in a yard. The first time it drove a square, it was sure it ended up back where it started. It was 1.2 m off. Then we fixed that and the endpoint looked perfect, but the robot had still driven the wrong square. Three bugs, one per layer: physics, mechanics, and our own analysis.

docs.title: Meet the mower
docs.text:
Everything is built from primitives and lives in git:

  • mowbot_description: a xacro model. Two driven rear wheels, a frictionless front caster, a blade under the deck, a front camera. The <gazebo> tags add the simulator plugins: DiffDrive (turns /cmd_vel into wheel speeds and publishes wheel odometry), JointStatePublisher, a velocity-controlled JointController for the blade, and OdometryPublisher for ground truth.
  • mowbot_gazebo: the yard world, a ros_gz_bridge config (Gazebo and ROS 2 are separate middlewares, so only topics listed in the bridge cross over), and sim.launch.py.
  • Two cameras rendered on the RTX 4080 with no window open: the mower's own (below), and a fixed "yard cam" for the shot above. scripts/camera_snapshot.py saves a frame as a PNG.

Ground truth is the superpower of simulation. A real mower never knows exactly where it is. Gazebo does. So every run publishes both /odom (what the robot thinks, integrated from wheel rotation, the way a real robot does it) and /ground_truth/odom (what actually happened). The gap between the two is the number Phase 3's localization has to shrink.

docs.title: Telemetry first, again
docs.text:
Following the rule from Phase 1, the contract in docs/telemetry.md came before the code. Two new things in it:

  1. Sim time. Every node runs with use_sim_time:=true and takes its time from Gazebo's /clock. That makes the results immune to the lying WSL clock, which is still about 8% slow after a WSL update and restart. But sim time starts at 0, which Kibana would plot in January 1970. The shipper now anchors it: @timestamp = wall time at start + sim time, and it keeps the raw value in sim.time_s.
  2. Real-time factor. The shipper reports rtf: sim seconds per wall second. It's been 1.00 on every run.

The experiment is make drive-run. A square_driver node drives a 3 m square with the blade on, steering only by odometry. The node records an MCAP bag, ships to Elasticsearch, and runs analysis/drive_report.py.

docs.title: Bug 1: the wheels skid in turns
docs.text:
First run:

| Speed tracking (worst leg) | within 5% of 0.5 m/s | 18.5% off      | FAIL |
| Odometry drift             | <= 0.5 m per 10 m    | 1.180 m        | FAIL |
| Loop closure (true pose)   | <= 0.3 m             | 1.192 m        | FAIL |

Odometry said the robot ended at (0.008, −0.008), a near-perfect square. Ground truth said (0.95, −0.72).

The speed failure was our bug: the cruise window included the driver's slow-down near each corner. After the fix: 0.500 m/s on every leg.

The drift was real, and the MCAP bag showed where it came from. A new debug aid, scripts/bag_probe.py, prints odometry against truth once per sim second:

     t  cmd w |  odom yaw |  true yaw
 106.6   0.60 |      96.6 |      98.3
 107.6   0.60 |     131.0 |     135.5
 108.6   0.52 |     165.3 |     174.5
 109.6   0.10 |     178.7 |    -170.9   <- the wheels have stopped; the body keeps turning
 110.6   0.00 |    -179.8 |    -169.3

Every 90° turn really rotated about 99°. The wheels lose grip and the body slides, so odometry, which only counts wheel rotation, never sees it. The usual Gazebo culprit is cylinder collision shapes on a plane: the contact solver gets unstable edge contacts. A sphere of the same radius touches the ground at exactly one point. We made the shape a knob (WHEELS=cylinder|sphere), the same way hysteresis was a knob in Experiment #1, and the sphere run went:

| Odometry drift          | 0.011 m | PASS |
| Loop closure (true pose)| 0.012 m | PASS |

That's 100 times better. All green. Except…

docs.title: Bug 2: the endpoint lied
docs.text:
We plotted the paths for the blog and saw it right away:

The middle panel is a perfect square, rotated 6.7°. A closed loop returns to its start whatever its rotation, so "end error 1.1 cm" was true, and meaningless. The worst error along the path was 48 cm.

Lesson: a checkpoint metric can hide a path error. drive_report now also checks the worst odometry-vs-truth gap anywhere along the path (≤ 0.10 m). Rerunning it on the "passing" run turned it into a FAIL, which is the right answer.

docs.title: Bug 3: Newton's third law
docs.text:
Where did 6.7° come from? Zooming the bag in to 0.1 s steps:

     t  cmd v |  odom yaw |  true yaw    true wz
   1.0   0.00 |      -0.0 |      -0.0      0.000
   1.1   0.50 |      -0.0 |      -5.5     -0.791
   1.2   0.50 |      -0.0 |      -6.7      0.000

One tenth of a second, at the exact moment the driver started the first leg. That's also when it switched the blade on: 0 to 300 rad/s (about 2,900 rpm) in one physics step. Spinning a blade up counter-clockwise twists the body clockwise. Negative yaw, as measured.

A hypothesis is cheap; an experiment settles it:

Run Blade Worst path error sq-sph-1 instant start 0.484 m sq-sph-noblade-2 off 0.010 m sq-sph-spinup-2 3 s soft start, then drive 0.013 m

The fix is what real mowers do: spin the blade up before moving, over a few seconds (blade_spinup_s, default 3). With cylinder wheels, the soft start still drifts 1.23 m, which shows the two bugs are independent.

docs.title: What broke along the way
docs.text:
• Orphan simulators. Run #2 put odometry at 42 m after 15 seconds. Four headless Gazebo servers were still running from earlier runs: launch stops the gz Ruby wrapper, but the real server process can outlive it. With host networking, gz-transport finds every server, so their /clock and /odom streams got mixed into one. Two fixes: GZ_PARTITION=<run_id> gives each run its own private gz-transport network, and make sim-clean runs before and after every sim target. (We tried killing the server from an OnShutdown handler first. Launch refuses to start new processes once it's shutting down.)
  • BLADE=0 crashed the driver. That's the Phase 1 int-vs-double gotcha again: launch args are YAML, so 0 is an int. declare_float() moved into the shared mowbot_telemetry package so every node can use it.
  • Determinism is a feature. The cylinder run reproduced to the millimetre: truth (0.952, −0.717) vs (0.951, −0.718). In simulation, A/B comparisons are exact.

docs.title: Lessons
docs.text:
1. Odometry is a belief, not a measurement of position. It can't see slip, and it's confidently wrong.
  2. Check the path, not just the destination. A loop that closes can still be the wrong loop.
  3. Physics engines model what you give them. Collision shapes and actuator torques have consequences that look like "the robot is bad at driving".
  4. Keep the raw recording. Every finding here came from replaying MCAP bags, not from the 2 Hz Elasticsearch samples.

Next: drive it by hand (make sim and make teleop), and a Kibana "Drive" dashboard. Then Phase 3: add realistic wheel noise and slip, and make the robot work out where it is.

docs.title: Experiments #2 and #3: Crash a node, kill the database
docs.text: Closing out Phase 1 meant answering two uncomfortable questions: does a crash show up anywhere except a scrolling terminal? And what happens to telemetry when Elasticsearch dies? We broke things on purpose to find out, and the breakage found three bugs we didn't plan for.

docs.title: New tools for breaking things
docs.text:
• Fault injection. battery_sim has a fault_crash_after_s parameter: make battery-run FAULT=60 crashes it at 60 s.
  • Launch-level telemetry. A crashed node can't report its own death, but ros2 launch watches every process. process_exit_telemetry() turns each unexpected exit into a process_exit event.
  • Two new analysis checks. Data completeness (no gaps longer than 3 s) and no unexpected process exits.
  • A launch_testing integration test that starts the real nodes and asserts on the events, including the injected crash. There are now 15 tests.
  • MCAP replay. make replay RUN_ID=... rebuilds a run in Elasticsearch from its bag, 10× faster, on simulated time. The replay of Experiment #1 reproduced the drain rate (0.1%) and the transitions exactly.

docs.title: Experiment #2: crash battery_sim at 60 s
docs.text:
| Drain rate (fraction/min) | 0.5000 | 0.4982 (0.4% off) | PASS |
| Unexpected process exits  | 0      | 1 (battery_sim-1 rc=1) | FAIL |

The crash went from the process, to launch, to a ROS event, to Elasticsearch, to the analysis and the Kibana "Process exits" panel. It took three attempts:

  1. Attempt 1 crashed for the wrong reason. FAULT=60 reached the node as the integer 60, and the parameter was declared as a double: InvalidParameterTypeException at startup. Launch arguments are parsed as YAML, so 60 ≠ 60.0. Now there's a declare_float() helper that accepts both.
  2. Our crash reporter made launch hang. Publishing from launch's ROS node during shutdown raised cannot use Destroyable because destruction was requested and, in one run, apparently left ros2 launch hung for 24 minutes after every process had exited. (We fixed the cause before reproducing the hang, so that link is our best reading, not proven.) Now exits are only reported while the system is running (those are the crashes), the reporter can never raise into launch, and every automated launch has a hard timeout -k 20 deadline.
  3. The shipper crashed while shutting down, because it read the ROS clock after ROS had shut down. It now falls back to wall time for its final stats.

docs.title: Experiment #3: stop Elasticsearch for 55 seconds mid-run
docs.text:
final stats: received 157, shipped 157, dropped 0, rejected 0, es_unavailable 68

Zero data lost. The shipper failed 68 flush attempts, buffered everything in memory, and drained the backlog the moment Elasticsearch came back. The robot side never noticed.

The new bottom row tells the whole story:

  • Shipper health (bottom left): buffered jumps to about 60 during the outage and returns to 0. dropped and rejected stay at 0.
  • Host clock (bottom middle): wall minus monotonic climbs about 130 s in 30 minutes. That's the clock that lied, now permanently on the dashboard.
  • Process exits (bottom right): the injected crash, with expected=false.

Both runs still fail data completeness, and that's honest: every gap lines up with the host clock's +2.9 s steps (we checked the outage window gap by gap against the MCAP bag). Until the clocksource is fixed, this machine's timestamps can't be trusted, and the analysis says so.

Lessons learned

  • Chaos experiments test the observability, not just the system. Our first crash test mostly proved that our crash reporting had bugs.
  • Shutdown paths are where telemetry code goes to die. Three of today's bugs lived there.
  • Every automated process needs a deadline. A hang that a human would notice in 5 seconds blocked an agent for 24 minutes.
  • Buffer, count, and prove it. received == shipped with dropped == 0 is a claim the dashboard can check.

docs.title: From simulation to the yard: the plan, the parts and the honest business case
docs.text: Chris went to watch TV and left one instruction: keep going. Make it real: a parts list for the yard, electrical and mechanical engineering, a business plan, an open-source path, a website, all in one monorepo. Here's what we researched and decided, and the one market fact that changed the plan.

docs.title: The fact that changed the plan
docs.text:
A wire-free RTK robot mower, the kind that navigates by centimetre-level GPS with no boundary wire, now sells for about $669–1,099 (Segway's Navimow i105N, depending on promotions). Our sensor parts list alone, a Raspberry Pi 5 at $175 after the 2026 memory-driven price rises plus a u-blox ZED-F9P RTK board at €172–211 (≈ $195–235), is most of the way there before we've bought a motor.

So Mowbot can't win as a cheaper mower. The business plan (docs/business/business-plan.md) is built on what closed products can't offer: you can read the code, there's no cloud, you can repair it, and it's a complete learning path. The order is open project first, then education, then a blade-less developer kit. A certified consumer product comes only with funding, insurance and a manufacturing partner.

docs.title: The hardware plan: brain transplant first
docs.text:
The dangerous parts of a robot mower are the blade guard, the body and the battery, and they're mechanical rather than software problems. Cheap commercial mowers have already solved them and been through certification. So the first real robot is a used YardForce Classic 500 with the open-source OpenMower mainboard and our ROS 2 stack, the best-supported conversion target in that community. Stages:

Stage What Blade H0 Simulation (now) simulated H1 Pi 5 + RTK + IMU on a garden cart; survey the lawn boundary none H2 Brain transplant: drive, map, dock unplugged H3 After the safety checklist passes on, supervised H4 Custom chassis, only if needed

docs.title: Engineering numbers, worked from physics
docs.text:
The electrical design (hardware/electrical/) sizes the drive: a 15 kg robot on a 15° lawn slope at 0.5 m/s needs about 52 N of traction and ≈ 4 N·m per wheel at 40 rpm, so geared or hub motors. The energy budget is about 55 W average (with the blade as the big unknown), so two hours of mowing plus a 30% reserve is about 150 Wh: a 7S, 6 Ah pack.

The most important circuit is the blade interlock: a series chain of normally-closed contacts (e-stop, lift, tilt, an MCU watchdog pulse, and the ROS request) feeding the blade controller's enable line. A cut wire reads as unsafe. A frozen program can leave a pin stuck high, but it can't keep toggling one. Software decides when to mow; hardware decides when it may.

The sim fed straight into the mechanical spec: the blade reaction-torque finding made "spin the blade up before moving" a firmware requirement.

docs.title: What we couldn't verify
docs.text: Honest gaps are written into the docs. We haven't read the paid safety standard, IEC 60335-2-107 (one summary says the blade must stop within 2 s of a lift; unconfirmed). We found no reliable used price for the YardForce. Free RTK corrections depend on your state. And the name "Mowbot" needs a trademark search before any public launch.

docs.title: The monorepo now
docs.text:
src/ (robot software) · analysis/ · hardware/ · docs/business/ · blog/ · website/ · observability/. The website is plain HTML, CSS and JS. Its hero is a canvas of the mower cutting stripes inside an RTK geofence, drawn at the sim's real scale (40 px per metre, a 0.36 m blade swath).

Next: back to the robot. Phase 3 gives the simulated mower an IMU and GPS, and makes it work out where it is.

docs.title: Experiment #1: Does hysteresis stop flapping?
docs.text: Our first real experiment, run the way all of them will be: change one parameter, tag each run with a run_id, and let the analysis and dashboard decide.

docs.title: The question
docs.text:
The battery monitor sorts readings into OK, LOW and CRITICAL. Real batteries are noisy (our sim adds ±0.5% Gaussian noise), so when the true level sits right at a threshold, a naive classifier bounces between levels. A mower that flips between "go home" and "keep mowing" is a mower that twitches in the middle of the lawn.

The textbook fix is hysteresis: worsen immediately, but only recover after passing the threshold plus a margin. We built it with a 2% margin. Does it actually matter?

docs.title: The setup
docs.text:
Two identical 4.5-minute runs, back to back, with the same random seed. Only one parameter changed:

make battery-run RUN_ID=20261108-1734-hyst-0.02 HYST=0.02   # A: as designed
make battery-run RUN_ID=20261108-1734-hyst-0.00 HYST=0.0    # B: control

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Run Measured drain vs. configured Level transitions Verdict A: hysteresis 0.02 0.2501 vs 0.2500 (0.0% off) OK → LOW → CRITICAL ✅ PASS B: hysteresis 0 0.2501 vs 0.2500 (0.0% off) OK → LOW → OK → LOW → CRITICAL → LOW → CRITICAL → LOW → CRITICAL ❌ FAIL

Without hysteresis the monitor changed its mind 8 times instead of 2. The flaps came in bursts within about 3 seconds of each threshold crossing (22:43:00.9, 01.9, 03.4, 03.9): exactly the window where the noise is bigger than the true drain per tick.

Reading the dashboard:

  • Battery % by run (top left): all runs drain in clean straight lines. The drain-rate fix from Phase 1 holds at 0.0% error.
  • Level changes per run (bottom left): the hysteresis-0 bar towers at 8. That chart was designed for exactly this question, before we had the data.
  • Analysis results (top right): the pass/fail verdicts written back into Elasticsearch by analysis/battery_report.py.
  • ROS log lines by level (bottom right): the WARN and ERROR spikes are the flaps, logged as they happened.

docs.title: Why this matters for a lawnmower
docs.text:
Every threshold decision the mower makes later works the same way: "battery low, go dock", "obstacle close, stop the blade", "GPS fix lost, slow down". Each will get the same treatment: a contract, a control run, and a chart that shows the failure mode.

Lessons learned

  • Design the chart that would show the failure before running the experiment. If you can't picture it, you don't know what you're testing.
  • Keep failing control runs. Run B is now a regression test for the hysteresis logic, and its data is in ES and in an MCAP bag forever.
  • Same seed, one changed parameter, a tagged run_id. That's the whole recipe.

docs.title: Know where you are: IMU, RTK GPS and two Kalman filters
docs.text: Phase 3 gave the mower a gyro and centimetre-level GPS, and fused them with its wheels. The fusion worked. Getting there meant catching a sensor configured in the wrong units, a ground truth that spikes, and a filter that started 5,700 km from the robot.

docs.title: The sensors, contract first
docs.text: Modelled on the H1 hardware in the parts list: a BNO085-class IMU at 100 Hz (gyro σ 0.002 rad/s) and a u-blox ZED-F9P with RTK corrections at 5 Hz (σ 1.5 cm). The antenna sits on a mast 0.19 m forward and 0.30 m up, because RTK reports the antenna, not the robot. analysis/sensor_report.py checks each sensor against its configuration, the same way the battery report did in Phase 1.

docs.title: Finding 1: "1.5 cm" of noise was 1.7 km
docs.text:
The first GNSS report said the fixes were 1,513 m off. Gazebo's NavSat sensor applies <noise> to latitude and longitude in degrees, so 0.015 meant 0.015°. And a degree isn't a fixed distance: at 40°N one degree of latitude is 111.0 km but one of longitude is 85.4 km, so no single number in degrees can mean "1.5 cm" in both directions.

Fix: Gazebo publishes a perfect fix on /gps/fix_raw, and a small gnss_noise node adds noise in metres, sets the RTK status and covariance, and (later) simulates outages. Result: σ 1.49 cm, bias 0.10 cm.

The lever arm matters: comparing the antenna's fixes with the robot's centre instead of the antenna gives an RMS error of 19.2 cm, 13 times the sensor noise. Every real build needs that offset measured and in the URDF.

docs.title: Finding 2: the ground truth spikes
docs.text: The gyro "residual" was 12 rad/s. The gyro was fine. Gazebo's ground-truth odometry reported a yaw rate of −628 rad/s for one sample, as the heading wrapped past ±180°. We difference the true rate from the true poses ourselves now. Then the residual was still 15× too big, but only during turns: a 100 Hz IMU sees the robot wobble as it pivots, and 50 Hz truth can't. So the report checks noise where truth is precise enough (σ 0.0022 vs 0.002 configured), plus the check that matters for navigation: the gyro integrated over the whole drive drifts 0.30° in 367° of turning.

docs.title: Finding 3: the filter started 5,700 km away
docs.text:
robot_localization runs two EKFs: local (wheels + gyro, smooth but drifting) and global (+ RTK, no long-term drift). On the first run the global estimate began at 5,726 km error. navsat_transform published one fix before it had applied the datum, and that single jump wrecked the filter's heading for 25 seconds (143° wrong). The fix is a Mahalanobis gate: reject any GNSS position more than 5σ from the current estimate. Real RTK needs the same gate for multipath jumps.

We also found that Gazebo's wheel odometry reports zero covariance, which tells a filter "I'm perfect". A wheel_odom node now republishes it with honest uncertainty, and with knobs for the most common real-world bug: a mis-measured wheel radius and track width.

docs.title: The experiment
docs.text:
Run Wheels only + gyro (local EKF) + RTK (global EKF) Perfect calibration 0.6 cm RMS 1.1 cm 2.1 cm (that's RTK's own noise) Radius +3%, track +5% 20.6 cm (max 29.5) 7.7 cm (max 12.4) 2.1 cm (max 5.9) …plus a 20 s RTK outage 20.6 cm 7.7 cm 3.8 cm (max 9.1)

What it shows: - The gyro fixes heading (4.5° → 0.2° RMS). Heading errors are what turn into big position errors. - RTK fixes position, and it doesn't care how badly the wheels are calibrated. - During an outage, the global filter drifts like the local one, then snaps back within about a second of RTK returning. In Phase 4 that becomes a rule: if RTK is lost for more than a few seconds, stop the blade and wait. - In a perfect sim, wheels alone (0.6 cm) beat RTK (2.1 cm). A simulator that's too kind hides the reason a sensor exists. That's why the knobs exist. - The local filter's error shrinks near the end only because errors partly cancel around a closed square. That's luck, not accuracy, and on a mowing pattern it won't happen.

docs.title: Bonus bug
docs.text:
An empty OUTAGES= became gnss_outages:= on the command line (the shell drops empty quotes) and launch refused to start. Every default run would have broken, and the experiment that was meant to run without outages caught it.

Next: the yard boundary as a GPS polygon, then Phase 4, mowing.

docs.title: Liquid chrome: designing a mower, and drawings that can't lie
docs.text: The brief was "a really slick mower", plus electrical diagrams, a circuit-board plan, software architecture, mechanical drawings and renders. Here's how a software project designs hardware: everything is generated from code, and the drawings check themselves.

docs.title: The shape, and the engineering it had to obey
docs.text:
The M1 is a procedural three.js model: about 300 lines of maths in website/js/mower3d.js, rendered to stills in headless Chromium and live in the browser on the website. Every design move answered a constraint:

  • Reverse teardrop. The first render had the wheels sticking out like add-ons. Making the shell widest over the axle, tapering to the nose, gave room to hide them.
  • Haunches. The tyres are 240 mm tall and the shell is 245 mm. A car designer's answer is haunches: smooth swells over each wheel. They hide the tyres and give it a crouch.
  • A crease you could only see in chrome. The outline's front and rear curves met with a curvature break. On a matte surface you'd never notice; a mirror shows it as a line. We blended the curves with a smoothstep.
  • The GNSS eye. A metallised chrome shell would block satellite signals. The RTK antenna sits under a dark glass window at the crown. (Non-conductive vacuum metallisation, used on phone housings, is the thing to test.)
  • The light seam. Partly status (cyan positioned, amber blade on, red fault), partly safety: a mirror reflects the lawn, and a robot you can't see is a robot you step on.

docs.title: Drawings generated from code
docs.text:
scripts/make_diagrams.py writes six SVG sheets: the power architecture, the blade interlock, the electronics block diagram, the software data flow, a circuit-board plan and a three-view general arrangement.

Two of them can't drift from reality:

  1. The software diagram checks itself. make ros-graph starts the sim and captures the live ROS graph: 13 nodes, 24 topics, who publishes and who subscribes. Every arrow the diagram draws is asserted against that capture. Rename a topic and the drawing fails to build instead of lying.
  2. The three-view is computed from the 3D model's maths, with silhouettes swept from the same shell function. It immediately caught a mismatch: the sim's GNSS antenna is 420 mm up, but the design puts it under the eye at about 240 mm. That changes the lever arm, so the sensor report needs a rerun when the sim model is updated.

docs.title: The circuit that matters most
docs.text: The Mowbot Carrier board plan puts everything safety-critical on one board: power entry, regulators, a Pico 2 safety microcontroller, the IMU, CAN for the motor controllers, and the interlock. The Raspberry Pi becomes replaceable compute. No firmware sits in the blade's critical path: a frozen program can't keep toggling a watchdog pulse.

docs.title: The plan grew
docs.text:
Chris added lidar ("I don't know how you safely do this without lidar"), object detection and recognition, and a companion iPhone app for the live view, lawn selection and editing, and command and control. They're all in PLAN.md. The short version: lidar becomes the primary obstacle sensor (Phase 3b), the camera says what the lidar found, and the app uses Bluetooth for pairing and basic control and local Wi-Fi for the live map. Bluetooth can't carry lidar.

Next: Phase 3b, lidar in the sim and an obstacle course.

docs.title: Phase 0: A GPU, a container, and a window on Windows
docs.text: Goal: one command builds a robotics environment, and it renders on the GPU, inside Docker, inside WSL, on a Windows laptop.

docs.title: Picking a stack (in 2026)
docs.text:
Chris last used ROS 2 a while ago. It's still the standard, so we chose:

Layer Choice Why Middleware ROS 2 Jazzy (LTS to 2029) Same Ubuntu (24.04) as the WSL host Simulator Gazebo Harmonic Jazzy's paired release, good for outdoor ground robots Observability Elasticsearch + Kibana 9.5.3 Chris loves Kibana dashboards Everything else Docker Compose + Makefile Repeatable, pinned, scriptable by an agent

We passed on Isaac Sim for now. It's gorgeous, but heavy, it isn't officially supported on WSL, and 12 GB of VRAM is tight.

docs.title: The interesting trick: OpenGL through WSL
docs.text:
CUDA in Docker on WSL is easy (gpus: all). OpenGL rendering is the subtle part: Gazebo needs a real GPU, or it silently falls back to slow CPU rendering (llvmpipe). The recipe:

devices: [/dev/dxg]                        # WSL's GPU paravirtualization device
volumes: [/usr/lib/wsl:/usr/lib/wsl:ro]    # Windows driver userspace libs
environment:
  GALLIUM_DRIVER: d3d12                     # Mesa -> Direct3D 12 -> NVIDIA
  MESA_D3D12_DEFAULT_ADAPTER_NAME: NVIDIA

And make gpu-check proves it:

NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4080 Laptop GPU
OpenGL renderer string: D3D12 (NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4080 Laptop GPU)
OpenGL core profile version string: 4.6 (Core Profile) Mesa 25.2.8

docs.title: What broke
docs.text:
• gz: command not found. Non-interactive shells skip .bashrc, so ROS was never sourced. Fixed with a tiny scripts/in_ros.sh wrapper that every make target goes through.
  • Kibana "unavailable". It's slow to start (about a minute of migrations), and with no healthcheck make up returned too early. We added a real healthcheck.
  • Kibana encryption keys were randomly generated on every start, which breaks saved objects across restarts. We pinned local-only keys.
  • Claude wrote a broken Makefile line (a bash -c quoting trick that would have launched an empty shell), caught it on review, and replaced it with the wrapper script. Pair programming goes both ways.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
make doctor     ✔ 6/6 host checks
make gpu-check  ✔ CUDA + OpenGL 4.6 on the 4080
make sim-smoke  ✔ 2000 physics steps, headless
make es-check   ✔ ES green, Kibana available

Lessons learned

  • Pin the base image by digest, not by tag. Tags move; digests don't.
  • A health check that isn't checked (--wait with no healthcheck) is just optimism.

docs.title: Phase 1: Telemetry before code
docs.text: Chris's rule for this phase: "Before we build something in code, maybe it should have new telemetry?" So before the first ROS node existed, we wrote down the questions we'd ask of its data.

docs.title: The working method
docs.text:
Contract → telemetry → node → dashboard → analysis. Every component gets a section in docs/telemetry.md:

  1. Questions. What will we want to know?
  2. Signals. Which topics and events answer them?
  3. Dashboard. Which Kibana panel shows it?
  4. Analysis. Which script checks it, with pass/fail?

docs.title: The architecture
docs.text:
ROS nodes ──topics──▶ es_shipper ──bulk──▶ Elasticsearch ──▶ Kibana
     └─ /mowbot/telemetry (events) ┘                    └──▶ analysis/*.py
     └──▶ ros2 bag (MCAP): raw ground truth, replayable
  • Nodes never talk to Elasticsearch. They publish ROS topics. If ES dies, the robot doesn't care.
  • es_shipper is config-driven (shipper.yaml: which topics, how many Hz). It has a bounded buffer, de-duplicates events by id, and reports its own stats.
  • Every run gets a run_id, so Kibana can compare runs side by side.
  • Analysis results are written back into ES, so pass/fail shows up on the dashboard.

The first real component is a battery: battery_sim drains a noisy simulated pack, and battery_monitor classifies it OK → LOW → CRITICAL with hysteresis.

docs.title: The telemetry paid for itself on the very first run
docs.text:
Our analysis script fits a line to the battery data and compares it to the configured drain rate. Run smoke-1:

| Drain rate (fraction/min) | 2.0000 | 1.8665 (6.7% off) | FAIL |

Why 6.7% slow? The simulator assumed its 2 Hz timer fires exactly every 0.5 s. Python timers fire late, so simulated time drifted behind real time. This is a classic robotics bug, and it would have been invisible without measurement. The fix is to measure dt from the clock on every tick:

Correction (later the same day)

The fix was right, but this diagnosis was wrong. The timers weren't late. This machine's clock was broken: after the WSL kernel update, the monotonic clock (which timers use) ran ~9% slow, and time sync stepped the wall clock forward ~2.9 s every ~32 s to compensate. See The clock that lied.

| Drain rate (fraction/min) | 2.0000 | 1.9981 (0.1% off) | PASS |

Two more bugs fell out of the same runs:

  • Double SIGINT. timeout signals the whole process group, and ros2 launch forwards the signal again, so every node died mid-cleanup. Fixed with timeout --foreground.
  • An rclpy quirk. A log call site can't change severity between calls (warning then error from the same line crashes the node). Fixed by using two call sites.

That last crash revealed a telemetry gap: the node death showed up only in the console, not in Elasticsearch. It's on the TODO list.

docs.title: Dashboards as code
docs.text:
The Kibana dashboard lives in git as observability/kibana/mowbot.ndjson. make kibana-import loads it, and make kibana-export saves UI edits back. One gotcha: hand-written saved objects need a typeMigrationVersion, or Kibana replays seven years of migrations on them and crashes.

To check the dashboard really renders, and not just that the import returned 200, Claude takes a headless Chromium screenshot (make screenshot, via a pinned Playwright container). Here's the first one, taken while a run was draining live:

Lessons learned

  • Never trust a timer's period. Measure elapsed time.
  • Write the analysis before trusting the code. Our first "working" simulator was 6.7% wrong.
  • An agent that can't see your screen needs a way to look: headless screenshots close the loop.

docs.title: The clock that lied
docs.text: We added one boring check to the analysis, "are there gaps in the data?", and it unravelled a bug in the machine, not the code. It also proved that an earlier diagnosis of ours was wrong.

docs.title: A boring check fails
docs.text:
To finish Phase 1, battery_report.py got a data completeness check: no gap longer than 3 s between /battery samples in Elasticsearch. We expected it to pass trivially. It failed on our "good" run from Experiment #1:

| Data completeness (max gap) | <= 3 s | 5.4 s | FAIL |

docs.title: Follow the data down the stack
docs.text:
Suspect 1: the shipper drops data. We have the ground truth, so we checked the MCAP bag directly (analysis/bag_gaps.py):

header stamp: 546 msgs over 294.0s; top gaps: [3.44, 3.43, 3.43, 3.43, 3.43]

The gaps were in the bag too, so the shipper was innocent. And they were suspiciously identical: 3.43 s, every ~33 s.

Suspect 2: the node stalls. We ran battery_sim alone with a control: a plain Python loop doing sleep(0.5) and timing itself with the monotonic clock. The control never stalled once. The node "stalled" on schedule.

The arithmetic that cracked it: 546 messages at 2 Hz is 273 s of ticks, but the timestamps spanned 294 s. The node wasn't missing ticks. Time itself was jumping forward between them.

docs.title: Catching the clock in the act
docs.text:
$ python3 scripts/clock_check.py 75
  t+  8.5s  wall clock stepped +2.932s
  t+ 40.8s  wall clock stepped +2.931s
  t+ 73.1s  wall clock stepped +2.930s
wall-vs-monotonic drift over 75s: +8.793s

$ cat /sys/devices/system/clocksource/clocksource0/current_clocksource
tsc        # WSL2 normally uses hyperv_clocksource_tsc_page

The WSL update that killed our first session installed kernel 6.18, and it booted with the tsc clocksource. Linux's monotonic clock runs about 9% slow on it. Time sync notices and steps the wall clock forward about 2.9 s every 32 s. ROS timestamps use wall time; timers use the slow monotonic clock.

docs.title: We had it wrong earlier
docs.text: In Phase 1 we blamed a 6.7% drain error on "Python timers firing late". We were wrong. The 40 s smoke run contained one clock step (about 3 s out of about 43 s), and that was the error. Measuring dt from the clock was still the right fix, for the wrong reason. The old post now carries a correction.

docs.title: Making it observable, forever
docs.text:
Where What make doctor Fails if the clocksource isn't hyperv_clocksource_tsc_page make clock-check Measures wall-clock steps over 40 s es_shipper stats Reports clock_offset_s (wall minus monotonic) every 10 s, charted in Kibana Analysis The completeness check stays: it flags untrustworthy timestamps, which matter as much as missing data

The host fix needs root, so it's left for the human:

# Immediate (until the next WSL restart):
echo hyperv_clocksource_tsc_page | sudo tee /sys/devices/system/clocksource/clocksource0/current_clocksource
# Persistent: in Windows, %UserProfile%\.wslconfig
# [wsl2]
# kernelCommandLine = clocksource=hyperv_clocksource_tsc_page

Update: the clocksource wasn't it

Chris switched to hyperv_clocksource_tsc_page, and the steps continued: still +2.93 s every 32 s. Measured against the Windows clock over 60 s: Windows 65.82 s, Linux wall 66.18 s, Linux monotonic 60.32 s. The kernel's timekeeping runs ~8.4% slow under every clocksource, and systemd-timesyncd (polling at its 32 s minimum) steps the wall clock to compensate. The likely culprit is the new WSL kernel itself. make doctor now measures the clock rate against Windows (scripts/clock_rate.py) instead of trusting the clocksource name. A check that passes while the problem persists is worse than no check.

Lessons learned

  • Keep the raw data. Without the MCAP bag we would have "fixed" the shipper.
  • Run a control. One sleep() loop separated "the node" from "the machine".
  • Do the arithmetic. Message count × period vs. timestamp span exposed the clock.
  • Correct the record. A devlog that hides its wrong turns teaches the wrong lessons.
  • For a robot, time is data. Gazebo will run on simulated time, but anything stamped with wall time inherits the host's clock bugs.

docs.title: The hedgehog test: why the mower needs to look down
docs.text: Chris put it simply: "I don't know how you safely do this without lidar." RTK knows where the mower is. It knows nothing about what's in front of it. So Phase 3b gave the mower two lidars and an obstacle course, and asked one question: what does each lidar fail to see?

docs.title: The physics budget, first
docs.text: At 0.5 m/s, with about 0.15 s to notice (a 10 Hz lidar plus processing) and 1 m/s² of braking, the mower needs 0.075 + 0.125 ≈ 0.20 m to stop. So the safety field is a corridor the robot's width plus 10 cm, out to 0.7 m past the nose (stop the drive and the blade), with a slow-down field out to 1.5 m.

docs.title: The safety gate
docs.text:
A new node, safety_gate, sits between every driver and the motors:

driver → /cmd_vel_raw, /blade/cmd_vel_raw → [safety_gate] → /cmd_vel, /blade/cmd_vel → robot

It can slow the robot, stop it, and stop the blade. It can never start the blade: it only passes through or zeroes what the driver asks for. On the real robot it's one layer above the hardware interlock, which doesn't trust it either.

docs.title: The course
docs.text: Six objects, one per run, 3 m ahead on the robot's path: a pole, a 20 cm toy box, a toddler lying across the path (25 cm tall), a 20 cm ball, a hedgehog (10 cm), and a garden hose (4 cm). Plus an empty control run, because a safety sensor that cries wolf gets switched off. Two lidars: - 2D: one horizontal scan plane in the nose, 15 cm above the grass. - 3D: 16 beams from −25° to +5°, 30 cm up, looking down at the lawn ahead.

docs.title: Results (make obstacle-course)
docs.text:
Obstacle 2D lidar 3D lidar pole stopped, 0.67 m to spare stopped, 0.67 m to spare box (20 cm) stopped, 0.68 m stopped, 0.67 m lying child (25 cm) stopped, 0.69 m stopped, 0.69 m ball (20 cm) stopped, 0.68 m stopped, 0.67 m hedgehog (10 cm) HIT, never seen stopped, 0.67 m hose (4 cm) HIT, never seen stopped, 0.67 m (seen at 1.25 m) nothing (control) no false stops no false stops

The 2D lidar's blind spot is everything shorter than its scan plane. On a lawn, that's exactly the stuff that matters: wildlife, hoses, toys, small children. A mower's safety lidar has to look down.

docs.title: The bug that faked a miss
docs.text: The first run said the pole wasn't seen, and the robot ended up 2.6 m past it. Gazebo's spawner ignores the pose written inside an SDF string and uses its own -x/-y/-z (default: the origin). The pole had spawned inside the robot. The report caught it because "clearance −2.61 m" isn't physically possible for a static pole.

docs.title: The honest caveat
docs.text: The simulated lawn is a perfectly flat plane, so "anything more than 3 cm above the ground" is a clean obstacle test. Real grass is 5–10 cm tall, bumpy and sloped. On a real lawn that rule sees obstacles everywhere. Separating grass from hedgehog is the actual hard problem, and it's next: realistic grass in the sim, ground segmentation, and a false-alarm rate as a first-class metric. Then moving obstacles: a dog crossing at full speed.

docs.title: Day 0: The session that vanished
docs.text: The project started with a disappearance. Chris had a Claude Code Remote Control session open on the Windows/WSL laptop, driven from a phone. Then it was gone.

docs.title: What actually happened
docs.text:
The forensics took three commands:

$ uptime
 16:57:09 up 0 min

$ last -x | head -3
reboot   system boot  6.18.33.2-micros  Sun Nov  8 16:56   still running
shutdown system down  6.6.114.1-micros  Sun Nov  8 16:46 - 16:56

The WSL VM had shut down at 16:46 and rebooted onto a new kernel (6.6 → 6.18). That's the signature of a WSL/Windows update. Every Linux process died with it, including the claude process that Remote Control was attached to. The conversation transcript was safe on disk (claude --resume can bring it back), but the live session was gone.

docs.title: Rescuing the prompt
docs.text:
The message Chris was about to send was still sitting in the phone's input box, so he screenshotted it before it was lost too:

I want to play around with robotics. Virtually... Once I tried to make an autonomous lawnmower. Let's do that again. But. We're doing it agentic from the start. Docker containers. Bash scripts. Repeatable processes. Infrastructure as code... Making sure it's fault tolerant to subscription limits with Claude.

docs.title: The lesson that shaped everything
docs.text:
If a reboot can delete a conversation, the conversation can't be where the project lives. So from minute one:

  • PROMPT.md holds the original ask, transcribed from those screenshots.
  • PLAN.md holds the roadmap as session-sized checkboxes.
  • PROGRESS.md holds the handoff note, always ending in "Next step".
  • CLAUDE.md holds instructions for any future Claude session: read PROGRESS.md first.
  • A commit at every milestone. The worst case is losing one milestone.

Lesson learned

Treat AI sessions like spot instances: they can vanish at any moment. Put the state in git.

docs.title: Bookkeeping, a diagram that refused to lie, and the plan for Phase 5
docs.text: Four smaller jobs: the ROS graph documentation, the GNSS static test for gate 1, build records in Elasticsearch, and a written plan for Phase 5 (perception), which is now up for review before any of it is built.

docs.title: The diagram that refused to lie
docs.text:
The software architecture diagram is generated, and every arrow it draws is checked against a capture of the live ROS graph. The capture was still taken from the old square-drive experiment, from Phase 2. Re-capturing it from a real mowing mission (18 nodes, 41 topics) made the diagram generator refuse to run:

AssertionError: square_driver doesn't subscribe to /odom in the live graph

That's the check doing its job: the diagram showed a robot that no longer exists, and nobody noticed for a day. It now shows the real chain: the mission sends *_raw commands, and every one of them passes safety_gate (lidar field, STOP latch, watchdog) before it reaches the robot.

docs.title: GNSS static test (gate 1)
docs.text:
The first acceptance test on real hardware will be the push-cart's GNSS on a tripod for 10 minutes. The script that will judge it now exists, and like the end-of-line test it reads only /gps/fix, so it judges a simulator bag and a real ZED-F9P bag the same way. "RTK fixed" means the fix status and a reported σ ≤ 5 cm, because u-blox drivers report RTK float with the same status, and only the covariance tells them apart.

gnss-static-1 (sim, no fix for the first 45 s) Expected Measured Time to RTK fixed ≤ 300 s 44.8 s Fixed after the first fix ≥ 95% 100% Scatter, 95% per axis ≤ ±3.0 cm ±2.9 cm

It passed by 1 mm, and that's not luck. The simulated receiver's noise is σ = 1.5 cm per axis, and 95% of a Gaussian lies within 1.96σ = 2.94 cm. Our sim is set right at the gate's limit. A real RTK receiver in the open should do better; if it doesn't, that's worth knowing before it's bolted into a mower.

docs.title: Build records, as data
docs.text:
Every robot gets a JSON build record in build-records/<serial>.json, and make builds validates them, indexes them into Elasticsearch (one document per robot, one per part), and prints what each robot is allowed to do:

SIM-0001: ok; end-of-line PASS; gates none; may drive blade-off: True; may mow supervised: False

The rule that matters: only results on the robot's current revisions count. Flash new software and the old end-of-line PASS and gate results become history; the permissions disappear until the tests are rerun. A unit test pins exactly that.

docs.title: The Phase 5 plan, for review
docs.text:
Phase 5 is "don't run over the dog". The plan is in docs/phase5-perception.md, and its first line is the most important decision: perception can only add caution, never remove it. A neural network may make the robot stop, slow down or keep further away, but it can never tell the lidar "that's only grass, carry on". That keeps an untestable component out of the safety chain, and it has an honest cost: a hedgehog lower than the grass is then caught only by the camera and by a rule that's cheap and certain, no mowing between dusk and dawn, when hedgehogs are out.

The order puts the deterministic work first: real grass in the simulator (the flat lawn has been flattering the lidar), then moving people and dogs (anything that moves is treated as a person, no camera needed), and only then the camera, the detector and the real-image dataset that's the only honest measure of its accuracy. Seven decisions in it are Chris's to make, starting with that first one.

docs.title: Two buttons, faster turns, and a simulator that stopped telling everyone the time
docs.text: Three small changes, tested in one simulator run instead of three: the physical buttons from the controls spec (docs/controls.md) now exist in the sim, the robot turns faster at the end of each stripe, and the simulator runs 2.4× faster than real time without changing a single result.

docs.title: Two buttons, no app
docs.text:
The rule from the plan: the phone is optional, the buttons are not. The robot has a red STOP and one HOME/GO button, plus a light ring. The gestures are a small, pure state machine (mowbot_ui/gestures.py) with one unit test per row of the gesture table:

Gesture Does STOP pressed Latch the stop: wheels and blade off. Nothing moves until it's released GO held 2 s while stopped Release the stop, into paused: it never drives off on its own GO short press Pause / resume GO held 2 s Go home and wait at the dock STOP + GO held 5 s Bluetooth pairing (the ring blinks blue) GO held 10 s Soft reset

In the sim, a button_player node presses the buttons from a script, timed from the mission's start, so a button experiment is repeatable. A new report, analysis/ui_report.py, checks each press against ground truth:

Check (ui-test-2) Expected Measured STOP pressed while mowing: standstill ≤ 1.0 s 0.22 s Blade below 10% of speed yes 0.02 s (the sim blade has no inertia: on hardware this is the number that matters, and it gets measured at gate 3) Moved while STOP latched ≤ 2 cm 0.0 cm Released STOP (GO held 2 s): moved before a resume 0 0.0 cm Light ring while latched red, solid red, solid GO held 2 s while mowing: docked yes after 25 s …then waits on the dock until GO yes yes: 104 s on the charger, then back to the exact spot it left

Found by the second run: the robot that wouldn't leave

After "go home", a short GO press is supposed to send the robot back out. In ui-test-1 it sat on the charger forever. The gesture machine had marked the robot not paused after "go home", so the short press sent pause, which the mission rightly ignores on the dock. Now "go home" counts as a hold, and a unit test pins the sequence.

The safety gate honours the latch itself, not the mission: while STOP is latched it publishes zero speed and zero blade every 0.1 s, whatever anything upstream asks for. On the real robot the button also cuts power in hardware; the software latch is the second layer, not the only one.

Found by the first run: a method name

The first run's button presses did nothing. The ui_controls node had died at launch: I'd named a method handle, which silently replaced rclpy's own Node.handle. The unit tests never constructed the node, so they passed. Now a smoke test constructs every node, and a 2-minute sim run isn't how we find a typo-class bug.

docs.title: Faster turns
docs.text:
At the end of each stripe the robot slowed to 0.2 m/s a full metre before the corner and pivoted at 0.6 rad/s. Turning cost about 30% of the mowing time. Rather than tune in the simulator (minutes per try), the offline replay swept the gains in seconds, with RTK-like noise:

Pivot Slow zone Slow speed Test patch time Worst cross-track 0.6 rad/s 1.0 m 0.2 m/s 475 s 17.8 cm (noisy replay) 1.0 rad/s 0.5 m 0.3 m/s 354 s (−25%) 15.9 cm 1.5 rad/s slower it overshoots and pivots again

Faster pivots aren't always faster: with 2 rad/s² of angular acceleration, 1.5 rad/s overshoots and turns back.

The replay of the whole back yard then found one spot 12.6 cm off the line: a U-turn with a short diagonal link between stripes. The robot pivoted at the first kink (148°) but only arced round the second (32°), because a pivot needs more than 40° of heading error. Slowing down didn't help; the arc was the problem. Now, at a corner's vertex, a pivot starts at 17°. Worst cross-track on the back yard: back under 10 cm.

Then the simulator, which is the judge:

Test patch Before (power-test-3) After (ui-test-2) Time in the MOW phase 484 s 428 s (−12%) Coverage of the reachable area 95.5% 97.3% Worst cross-track while mowing — 8.4 cm (limit 15) Localization error — 2.2 cm RMS, 7.0 cm max

Twelve per cent, not the twenty-five the replay promised. We haven't pinned down why. Our best guess: the replay's robot is a kinematic model that follows the acceleration limits exactly and never slips, and the faster gains spend more of each turn accelerating and braking, where the model and Gazebo differ most. (Both runs were also interrupted mid-mission, one by a low battery and one by the buttons, so they aren't perfectly like for like.) The replay is still the right tool for ranking gains in seconds; the sim gives the number we quote.

docs.title: A faster simulator
docs.text:
Every node runs on simulation time, so the simulator doesn't have to run at real time: a new rtf launch argument sets Gazebo's real-time factor, and 0 means "as fast as you can". The first try only reached 1.7× real time, on a 32-core machine that was mostly idle. So: what was busy? top, during a run:

Process CPU before Why Gazebo (physics + sensors) 200% the actual simulation each of ~12 Python nodes 70–110% woken by /clock, 1,714 times a second the Elasticsearch shipper 110% decoding every /joint_states message before throttling to 2 Hz

Gazebo publishes /clock and /joint_states once per 1 ms physics step. At 1.7× that's 1.7 kHz, and every node on sim time subscribes to /clock. Most of the machine was spent telling a dozen programs what time it was.

The fix is one small node, sim_throttle: Gazebo's clock and joint states now arrive as /clock_raw and /joint_states_raw, and it republishes them at 100 Hz and 50 Hz of sim time. Nothing needs finer: the fastest control loop is 20 Hz, and every sensor message carries Gazebo's own timestamp. (The joint-state plugin has an update_rate setting; we tried it first. This Gazebo version ignores it, measured at 1000 Hz.)

We also stopped rendering what nobody looks at: lean:=true (the default for make mow-run) drops the cameras and the lidar the safety gate isn't using. That one barely mattered, about 5%: a reminder to measure before optimising.

Same scripted test-patch mission (~600 s of sim time) Whole make mow-run, wall time Real-time factor while mowing real time (before) ~11 min (estimated: 600 s + setup and reports) 1.0× rtf:=0 (ui-test-1, stopped early by a bug) — 1.7× + lean (ui-test-2) 436 s 1.8× + sim_throttle (ui-test-3) 344 s ≈ 2.4×

The results didn't change: 97.3% vs 97.2% coverage, 2.2 vs 2.3 cm localization error, 0.22 vs 0.21 s to stop. Now the physics itself is the busiest process. The next step would be a coarser physics step, which changes the dynamics, so it needs its own experiment, not a speed tweak.

docs.title: The back yard, and a bug that wasn't the new gains
docs.text:
With a 2.4× simulator, the whole back yard (252 m², 830 m of path, 38 minutes of mowing) takes 16 minutes of wall time instead of about 40. Its first run, backyard-2, covered 98.7% of the reachable lawn, but failed one check: 16.2 cm off the line, against a 15 cm limit.

The new gains were the obvious suspect. They weren't to blame. The coverage report now says where the worst point is (8.42, 6.99), and the recorded bag says what happened there:

  1. Running along the outer lap at 0.5 m/s, 0.9 m short of a corner, the mission suddenly commanded a pivot.
  2. Its position estimate was fine (2 cm off), and so was its heading. Fed the same poses offline, the follower did the same thing, so it was deterministic.
  3. The cause was Polyline.project, which finds "how far along the path am I". It searches only forward, so the robot can never skip to a neighbouring stripe, and it rejected any point more than 5 cm behind the last answer. An RTK correction had just moved the estimate 6 cm backwards. The robot's own spot on the lap was rejected, and the only candidate left in the 1.5 m search window was the corner, 1.4 m away. So "how far along" jumped to the corner, and the robot turned for a corner it hadn't reached.

This needs two coincidences, a backwards correction just as a corner enters the window, which is why earlier runs never showed it. The fix: when the robot is slightly behind, hold the position where it was instead of throwing the candidate away. A unit test reproduces the exact geometry.

Back yard backyard-2 backyard-3 (the fix) Coverage of the reachable area 98.7% 99.3% Worst cross-track while mowing 16.2 cm ❌ 9.7 cm Keep-out incursions 0 0 Localization 2.5 cm RMS 2.5 cm RMS Docked at the end first try first try Sim time / wall time 2273 s / 989 s 2207 s / 953 s

docs.title: Batching
docs.text: The three changes went into one run: the buttons, the new gains and the speed-up are all measured by the same recorded bag, by four reports (coverage, power, localization, controls). A failure in any of them is still attributable, because each report checks one thing.

docs.title: The end-of-line test, and the robot that kept driving
docs.text: A factory doesn't ship a product because each part passed its own test. At the end of the line, one last test checks the assembled thing: every sensor, every motor, every way it can stop. Our robot now has one: a single script, make eol-run, that drives the robot through 33 checks and prints PASS or FAIL. It found two real problems on its first two runs, in a simulator we thought we knew well.

docs.title: One script, the robot's own sensors
docs.text:
The rule that shaped it: the end-of-line test may only use what the real robot has. Every other report in this devlog compares the robot against Gazebo's ground truth, which a real lawn doesn't have. This one uses the wheel encoders, the IMU, the GNSS, the lidar and the battery, so the script that passes in the simulator is the same script that will run on the real robot, unchanged.

It drives through the *_raw command topics like any mission, so every command goes through the safety gate: the test exercises the whole chain, not just the motors.

Step What it does Pass if 1 sensors Listens for 5 s, robot still Every topic at ≥ 90% of its rate; gravity 9.81 m/s²; RTK fixed; a sane 7S battery 2 wheels Forward, pivot left, pivot right Each wheel at the speed the command implies, with the right sign; IMU yaw rate agrees 3 blade Soft start, then off 90% speed in ≤ 4 s; below 10% in ≤ 2 s 4 STOP Presses STOP at 0.3 m/s with the blade on, while the driver keeps commanding motion Standstill ≤ 1 s; nothing moves while latched; release leaves it stopped 5 watchdog Drives with the blade on, then the driver goes silent Drive stops ≤ 1 s, blade ≤ 3 s 6 obstacle Drives at a box and keeps asking to go on The safety gate stops it ≥ 10 cm short 7 manual Lift, tilt, bumper, interlock connectors, hung microcontroller A person does these and signs the build record

Step 2 is the one that will earn its keep on hardware: a swapped motor connector or an IMU mounted backwards looks fine on a bench and turns the robot in circles on a lawn. Checking the sign of every wheel against the gyro catches both in three seconds.

docs.title: eol-1: the robot that kept driving
docs.text:
The first run passed 25 of 27 automatic checks. The two failures were step 5: when the driver went silent, the robot didn't stop. It never stopped. It carried on at 0.3 m/s until the lidar saw the box and the safety gate stopped it 0.69 m short.

Gazebo's drive plugin keeps executing the last command it received, and so do many real motor controllers. Our safety gate passed commands through but never asked how old they were. So a mission that crashed, hung or lost its connection mid-stripe would have left the robot driving, blade spinning, in a straight line, with only the lidar between it and the fence.

The fix is a rule: commands are a heartbeat. A driver that wants motion has to keep saying so. If the gate hears nothing for 0.5 s (the limit our safety analysis already named for the motor controller) it sends zero, for the drive and the blade separately. A zero command needs no watchdog, so a parked robot isn't flooding the log. One driver, the old square-drive experiment, sent its blade command only once and relied on it sticking; it now repeats it every tick.

docs.title: eol-2: the blade that twisted the robot
docs.text:
With the watchdog, step 5 passed (drive stopped in 0.51 s). Step 6 now failed in a new way: the robot saw nothing ahead but the fence 8 m away, and the box was not in front of it. The bag's ground-truth heading told the story:

Sim time What happened Heading (ground truth) 29 s driving straight, blade on 0.1° 31 s STOP pressed: blade cut 7.9° 47 s driver silent: watchdog cuts the blade 15.9°

Each blade stop twisted the whole robot by 8°. The simulated blade motor had unlimited torque: told to stop, it stopped the blade within one 1 ms physics step. The blade disc stores 0.0081 kg·m² × 300 rad/s of angular momentum; dumping that in a millisecond means a reaction of about 2,400 N·m on the chassis, which overpowers the tyres. After two stops the robot pointed 16° off and drove right past the box.

We met this physics before, on the other side: the instant blade start that rotated the square by 6.7°. That finding was real physics, but with an unrealistically strong motor. A real blade motor has a torque limit and takes most of a second to stop. The simulated one now does too: torque control, capped at ±3 N·m.

Run Watchdog: drive stops Blade stop (commanded) Twist per blade stop Result eol-1 never 0.01 s 8° FAIL eol-2 (+ watchdog) 0.51 s 0.01 s 8° FAIL (missed the box) eol-3 (+ torque-limited blade) 0.54 s 0.75 s < 0.1° PASS

The blade stop time is now 0.75 s instead of 0.01 s. The old number was never a believable one to test against; the last post already said the sim blade had no inertia. Also honest: with the motor capped, an instant start no longer twists the simulated robot much either. We keep the soft start (it's kinder to the motor and the battery), but its simulator evidence was partly an artefact.

The 2 s blade-stop limit is our target, not a measurement. Gate 3 measures the real motor, and the limit gets set from that, in the verification page, never quietly in code.

docs.title: eol-4: the pivots don't cancel
docs.text:
eol-3 left one loose end: pivoting left for 2 s then right for 2 s should end where it started, but the robot ended 6.5° off. The IMU-rate checks passed (within 15%), and nothing else depends on the pivots being symmetric. Rather than chase it, the test now uses the robot's own gyro to turn back to the start heading before step 6, so the box is always in front of it. The report records how far off it was.

eol-4: the gyro said −6.1° after the pivots, the robot turned back, and every automatic check passed again (blade stop 0.74 s, watchdog 0.52 s, 19 cm short of the box).

docs.title: Did the changes break mowing?
docs.text:
A watchdog that cuts a silent driver could also cut a quiet one: a mission that sends a command only when it changes would now stop every 0.5 s. So the same scripted test-patch mission as last time (ui-test-3: STOP press, release, go home, resume) ran again, with all four reports:

Test patch ui-test-3 (before) ui-test-4 (watchdog + torque-limited blade) Coverage of the reachable area 97.3% 96.9% Worst cross-track 8.4 cm 8.2 cm Localization 2.2 cm RMS 2.4 cm RMS STOP: standstill / blade below 10% 0.22 s / 0.02 s 0.04 s / 0.76 s Dockings first try 2 of 2, first try Watchdog firings during the mission — 0

The mission already sends a command every tick, so the watchdog never fired. The STOP blade time is now the believable 0.76 s.

docs.title: The build manual grew
docs.text:
• End-of-line test: what it checks, how to run it on a real robot (blade:=false lidar:=false on the H2 build: no blade, no lidar yet), and the build-record entry it writes.
  • H2: brain transplant and H3: blade on: drafts, written before the hardware exists, from the build guide and the safety checklist. The order and the pass criteria are fixed; the physical how-to gets rewritten from the real build.

docs.title: Going home: a battery that runs down, a dock that has to be hit to 4 cm
docs.text: A mower that mows until the battery dies in the middle of the lawn isn't a product. This milestone gave the simulated mower a battery that drains by what it's actually doing, a dock with charging contacts, and a mission that goes home when it must, charges, and comes back to exactly where it stopped. It took three runs, and the two failures were both about the last few centimetres.

docs.title: A battery with physics, not a timer
docs.text:
The Phase 1 battery drained at a fixed rate. Now mowbot_power/pack.py turns the robot's real activity into watts, using the energy budget from the electrical design:

  • 9 W for the computer and sensors, always
  • drive: 15 N of rolling resistance × wheel speed ÷ 60% efficiency, plus a scrub term for pivots (tyres dragged sideways), so a pivot costs more than rolling at the same wheel speed
  • blade: 30 W at full speed

That gives 52 W mowing straight, against the budget's ≈ 55 W. The pack is 7 cells of Li-ion at 6 Ah (155 Wh) with an open-circuit-voltage curve, sag under load, and a charger that tapers and terminates like a real one. Every number is a parameter, because every one of them gets replaced by a measurement when the real robot exists.

For the experiment I gave the mower a toy pack (0.2 Ah), so a 10-minute sim mission has to go home once.

docs.title: The mission becomes a state machine
docs.text:
LEAVE ─▶ MOW ─(battery low)─▶ SPINDOWN ─▶ RETURN ─▶ DOCK ─▶ CHARGE ─▶ LEAVE ─▶ RESUME ─▶ MOW ─(done)─▶ … ─▶ DOCK
                                                    ▲   │
                                                    └ REDOCK (no contact: back out 0.8 m, try again, max 3)

Some rules that came from thinking about the real yard:

  • When to go home is reserve (15%) + 1.5 × the energy for the trip, not a fixed percentage: far from the dock, leave earlier.
  • Only from a safe spot. If the battery runs low while the robot is on the lap 0.40 m from the flowerbed, turning for home there would swing the nose into the bed. It mows on to the next point where a pivot is safe.
  • Blade off and stopped before leaving the lawn. A 3 s spin-down standing still.
  • Reversing off the dock is blind (the lidar looks forward), so it's slow (0.15 m/s), short, and only along the path it drove in on. A rear sensor is on the plan.

docs.title: Run 1: the heading that wandered off while charging
docs.text:
power-test-1 went home at 17%, docked, charged, resumed and finished. The power report passed. But the localization report failed: a 17.7 cm position error, while the robot was reversing straight off the dock. The estimated heading swung to 43° and back in three seconds; the gyro and wheels both said it wasn't turning.

With no compass, heading is only observable while the robot moves: RTK positions over time. Five minutes parked on the charger, the filter's heading uncertainty grew with every prediction step, and the first RTK fixes after it moved were allowed to swing it. The fix is what real mowers do: the dock is a landmark. Seated on the contacts, the robot's heading is the dock's heading, to a few degrees. A small node (dock_anchor) feeds that to the global EKF while the robot is docked.

docs.title: Run 2: pure pursuit's dirty secret
docs.text:
power-test-2 docked, lost contact 1.1 s later, and failed all three retries. Ground truth showed why: in the last 30 cm the robot swung its heading from +6° to −10° at up to 1 rad/s, touched the contacts at −5°, and its turning momentum carried it to −23°, off the 8° window.

Pure pursuit steers with curvature 2·y / L², where L is the distance to the aim point. Clamp the aim point to the end of the path and, as the robot arrives, L goes to zero: 1 cm of RTK noise at 5 cm out is a curvature of 8. The offline docking test hadn't caught it because its localization was perfect. Two fixes:

  • the path now extends past its end, so the aim point stays a full lookahead away
  • the replay tool gained localization noise (1.5 cm, 0.5°), and a new test checks the turn rate in the last 30 cm. I checked that the test fails on the old code before trusting it.

docs.title: Run 3: home and back
docs.text:
Check power-test-3 Coverage of the reachable area 95.5% (PASS) Keep-out incursions 0 Lowest battery 13.4% (floor 10%) Dockings 2, one needed a second attempt; contact error 1.1 cm / 0.4° and 0.4 cm / 0.2° Resumed where it stopped yes (s = 84.0 m) Localization max error 6.8 cm (was 17.7 cm)

And the first real energy number: mowing costs about 208 mWh per m² in this model, and the trips home add 10%. One 155 Wh design pack would mow about 576 m² per charge. That's a number to check with a wattmeter on a real lawn, which is exactly why the report prints it.

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• The last centimetre is a different problem from the last metre. Path following that's excellent at mowing (8 cm) fell apart at the dock, because the maths of the controller changes as the target gets close.
  • Test with the noise in. A perfect-localization test proved the geometry and hid the instability.
  • Landmarks you already own are free. The dock fixes position for charging and heading for localization.

Next: the full back yard, and physical buttons (STOP, HOME/GO) and a status light, simulated first.

docs.title: Mowing patterns: five runs to mow a lawn without touching the flowerbed
docs.text: Phase 4 is the one Chris was waiting for: the robot plans a mowing pattern for a lawn and mows it. A planner turns the lawn (a GeoJSON polygon with keep-outs) into a path, a follower drives it on the RTK pose, and a report says, with ground truth, what got cut and whether anything went wrong. The first run finished the lawn. It also drove into the flowerbed 24 times. This post is about the four fixes between that run and a clean one, and about the tool that made the last fixes take seconds instead of minutes.

docs.title: The pattern
docs.text:
The planner (mowbot_mowing/planner.py) is pure geometry with shapely, no ROS, so it's unit-tested like any Python library:

  1. Headland laps first. Two laps around the inside of the lawn edge, the first at 0.35 m (half the robot's width plus 5 cm), the second one stripe further in. Edges first is what every good mower does: the stripes can then end short of the edge and turn on grass that's already cut.
  2. Stripes (boustrophedon, "the way an ox ploughs") at 0.324 m: the 0.36 m blade with 10% overlap. They end 0.75 m from keep-outs, because the robot's nose is 0.49 m ahead of the axle.
  3. Transits between them go round keep-outs on a visibility graph (Dijkstra over the free area's corners).

The follower (coverage_mission) is pure pursuit: aim at a point 0.5 m further along the path and steer on the arc that reaches it. The blade spins up over 3 s before the robot moves (the twisted-square lesson is not forgotten).

docs.title: The report: what does "mowed" mean?
docs.text:
analysis/coverage_report.py paints a 5 cm grid. A cell is cut when the blade disc (Ø 0.36 m, 0.19 m ahead of the axle) passes over it while the blade's measured speed is above 100 rad/s, using ground truth, not what the robot believes. Then the checks:

Check Threshold Why Mission completed mission_done not aborted, not stuck Coverage of the reachable area ≥ 95% what the plan's blade path can cut Keep-out incursions, body 0 the footprint never touches the flowerbed Keep-out incursions, blade 0 obviously Cross-track error (max) ≤ 0.15 m how far the robot wanders from the plan

Whole-lawn coverage is reported too, but it can't reach 100%: the band along fences and beds that the body can't reach is trimmer territory, as on every robot mower.

docs.title: Five runs
docs.text: Run Body in the bed Coverage (reachable) Worst cross-track What we changed after it mow-test-1 24 95.9% 0.146 m keep-out "islands" + 10 cm margin mow-test-2 0 95.7% 0.157 m never aim past a sharp corner mow-test-3 0 96.2% 0.152 m corners = heading change over 30 cm mow-test-4 0 95.1% 0.158 m pivot hysteresis, offline replay tool mow-test-5 0 96.9% 0.082 m (RMS 0.016) PASS

docs.title: Run 1: the nose is not the axle
docs.text:
The body hit the flowerbed 24 times; the blade never did. A small diagnostic script listed every incursion with its time, position and speed, and two causes fell out:

  • The deep ones (up to 32 cm²): a transit drove straight at the bed to reach the start of the lap around it, then turned 90°. The axle stopped exactly on the lap, 0.35 m from the bed. The nose, 0.49 m ahead, was over the bed.
  • The grazes (under 1 cm²): pure pursuit cuts the corners of a curve a little, and 5 cm of margin wasn't enough.

The fix is a rule: never drive at a keep-out. Each flowerbed is now an island with two laps. The robot reaches the outer lap (0.72 m out) first. That's far enough that it can pivot safely: a pivot swings the nose's corners round a circle of radius √(0.49² + 0.30²) = 0.575 m. Then it slides onto the inner lap (0.40 m now, 10 cm of margin) while driving round, never pointing at the bed, and slides back out the same way.

How gentle does the slide have to be? Driving at angle θ to the lap puts the inner front corner 0.30·cos θ + 0.49·sin θ sideways of the path. My first try slid in over 1 m (θ ≈ 18°): that's 0.44 m, more than the 0.40 m lap. I didn't work that out by thinking; a new unit test did. It sweeps the robot's real footprint along every segment of the plan (and the full 0.575 m circle at every pivot) and asserts it never touches the bed. The slide is now 2 m long (θ ≈ 9°, 0.37 m) and follows the lap's curve instead of cutting across it as one straight chord.

Run 2: zero incursions.

docs.title: Runs 2 to 4: chasing two centimetres
docs.text:
Runs 2, 3 and 4 failed on cross-track error by 2 to 8 mm. That's not a safety problem, but a threshold is a threshold, and each miss had a real cause:

  • Run 2: pure pursuit aims 0.5 m ahead. Near a stripe end that point is already on the next stripe, so the robot started turning early and cut the corner. Fix: never aim past a sharp corner. Drive to it, pivot, carry on.
  • Run 3: the corner fix worked (only 4 samples out of 4,000 above 10 cm), except on one tight curve made of many 10° steps. No single step looked sharp. Fix: "sharp" now means the heading turns more than 45° (later 30°) within the next 30 cm of path.
  • Run 4: still 0.158 m. Here I compared the robot's own estimate with ground truth at the worst moments: both showed the same error, so localization (2 cm) wasn't to blame. The follower was.

docs.title: The tool that should have come first
docs.text:
Every sim run costs about 7 minutes. Four of those to chase a follower bug is slow, and each one only tells you that it failed. So I pulled the control law out of the ROS node into a pure function, steer(), and wrote mowbot_mowing/replay.py: a 40-line kinematic robot (the sim's acceleration limits, 20 Hz, no physics) that drives the follower over the whole plan in under a second.

It reproduced run 4's problem immediately (0.133 m, offline) and printed the moments around it:

t=71.60 (1.35,-2.41) v=0.00 w=-0.60     pivoting at the corner...
t=71.80 (1.38,-2.41) v=0.20 w=-0.61     ...stops pivoting at 40° off and drives away at an angle
t=72.20 (1.52,-2.45) v=0.50 w=-0.45     full speed, still swinging wide

The pivot ended as soon as the heading error dropped under 40° (0.7 rad), and the robot left the corner at an angle. The next vertex was a 45° jog, and the "sharp" test was > 45°, so it didn't slow down either. The fix is hysteresis, the same idea as experiment #1: start a pivot above 40°, end it only below 6°. And corners now count from 30°. Offline worst case: 0.059 m. The price is time: the careful pivots make the replay about 20% slower.

The replay is now a unit test (test_replay.py, threshold 0.08 m), so a follower change that gets sloppy fails in make test before anyone spends a sim run on it. The sim stays the judge, since it has slip, EKF lag and real dynamics, but it no longer has to be the debugger.

docs.title: The coverage map
docs.text: Run 5. Green is grass the blade actually passed over (ground truth, blade at speed), tan is grass it didn't; the blue line is the plan. 96.9% of what the plan can reach got cut; the tan band around the edges and the bed is the 17–22 cm the body can't reach. It took 524 s of sim time against run 4's 405 s: the careful pivots cost 30%, and buying some of that back (faster pivots, smoother joins) is on the list. For comparison, run 1, the one that drove its nose into the flowerbed (its inner lap was 0.35 m from the bed, reached nose-first):

docs.title: And then the back yard
docs.text:
With the test patch passing, I pointed the planner at the full L-shaped back yard (257 m², the flowerbed and a tree) and checked it offline first: footprint sweep plus replay. It was safe, but 32% of the path was transit. Stripes cut in two by a keep-out were mowed nearest-piece-first, and the leftovers had the robot criss-crossing the yard to collect them.

The fix is the textbook one, boustrophedon cell decomposition: walk down the rows, and wherever a row splits into two pieces (a keep-out) or two pieces merge, start a new cell. Inside a cell every row is one unbroken stripe, so it mows end to end as a snake. Then go to the nearest unmowed cell. Transit fell from 360 m to 49 m, and the replayed mission from 52 to 39 minutes. test_replay.py now fails if the back yard's transit share goes above 10%. The sim run of the back yard is next.

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• A robot is a shape, not a point. The planner reasoned about the axle; the flowerbed met the nose. Every geometry check now uses the real footprint, and the pivot circle where the robot turns.
  • Reach for a cheap simulator of the expensive simulator. Gazebo answers "does it work?". A 40-line kinematic model answers "why not?", a thousand times faster.
  • Thresholds that fail by millimetres are still worth chasing. Each near-miss here was a real behaviour (aiming past corners, missing tight curves, leaving pivots early), and fixing them halved the typical error.

Next: the back yard in the sim, and a battery that runs down, so the mower has to go home.

docs.title: The hedgehog that vanished: a safety regression I introduced, and how the course caught it
docs.text: Two nights ago the hedgehog test showed the 3D lidar stopping for every obstacle on the course. Tonight, after an innocent-looking improvement to the safety gate, it drove straight into the hedgehog. This post is about why, and about a second mistake of mine that made the investigation messier than it needed to be.

docs.title: The improvement
docs.text:
The safety gate used a fixed protective field: stop if anything is within 0.7 m of the nose. That's wasteful when the mower is creeping at 0.2 m/s: it stops far earlier than physics requires, which makes mowing near hedges and fences miserable. So for the mowing work I made the field speed-dependent: margin + 2 × the stopping distance (reaction time plus braking), capped at 0.7 m. At 0.5 m/s that's 0.5 m; at 0.2 m/s, 0.2 m.

The unit tests passed. The square-drive regression passed. I moved on to mowing.

docs.title: The re-run
docs.text:
Before committing the mowing work I re-ran the full obstacle course (make obstacle-course, 7 obstacles × 2 lidars) as a regression check. The 3D lidar hit the hedgehog and the hose. The report said:

Check course-a (fixed field) course-b (speed-dependent) First seen (ahead of the nose) 1.47 m 1.47 m Detected (inside the stop field) yes no Clearance after stopping 0.67 m -0.06 m (collision)

Seen at the same distance, never stopped. The geometry explains it. The 3D lidar sits 0.30 m up and looks down at most 25°. Anything lower than the beam is invisible, and the lowest beam reaches a 4 cm hose only (0.30 − 0.04) / tan 25° = 0.56 m out from the lidar, which is 0.47 m ahead of the nose. Closer than that, a low object is under the beams.

So: the hedgehog appears at 1.47 m, inside the slow field. The robot slows to 0.2 m/s, so the stop field shrinks to 0.2 m. The hedgehog crosses 0.47 m and drops out of view, still 0.27 m before it would have entered the stop field. Nothing in view, so: clear, carry on. Bump.

The old fixed 0.7 m field happened to be larger than the blind zone, so it worked by accident.

docs.title: The fix: the sensor's geometry sets a floor
docs.text:
The stop field may shrink with speed, but never into the sensor's blind range. fields.blind_range() computes it from the lidar's mount (looked up from TF, so moving the lidar on the URDF updates it) and its lowest beam, for the smallest obstacle we promise to detect (the 4 cm hose). The gate floors the field at blind range + 10 cm. A 2D lidar has no near blind zone (it just can't see anything lower than itself, which is why it misses the hedgehog by design).

Course-c, the full course again:

Obstacle 2D lidar 3D lidar pole stopped, 0.20 m to spare stopped, 0.55 m to spare box stopped, 0.20 m stopped, 0.55 m child stopped, 0.19 m stopped, 0.55 m ball stopped, 0.18 m stopped, 0.55 m hedgehog HIT (too low to see) stopped, 0.55 m hose HIT (too low to see) stopped, 0.54 m none (control) no false stops no false stops

The deeper fix is memory: an obstacle that was seen and then entered the blind zone hasn't gone away. A short-lived obstacle map in the odometry frame would handle that, and it's now on the plan for the perception phase.

docs.title: The second mistake: two simulators in one box
docs.text:
While investigating, I re-ran the two runs that had failed in course-b. Their reports had crashed (no telemetry in the bag at all), so I assumed a flaky start and re-ran them by hand. They failed again, differently: Gazebo died 0.27 s after starting. It took me a while to see why: the course was still running in the background. Every sim target starts with make sim-clean, which kills every Gazebo server in the container. My re-runs and the course were killing each other's simulators, and four runs were spoiled before I noticed.

That explains the spoiled re-runs, but not the two original failures, where Gazebo started yet never published a single /clock message in 120 s.
