Those coincided with a runaway unit test of mine (a charging loop that never terminated) pinning a CPU core in the same container, but I can't prove the connection, so it goes in the known-quirks list: if a run's report says there's no telemetry at all, check launch.log for /clock before believing the result. Every run since, with nothing else in the container, has started cleanly.

Now sim targets run under a lock (scripts/sim_lock.sh, flock on /tmp/mowbot-sim.lock). A second run refuses to start, and sim_clean.sh refuses to kill anything while a run holds the lock. One detail mattered: flock -o, so the lock isn't inherited by Gazebo itself, because a stray server left behind must never hold the lock that would stop sim-clean from killing it.

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• Every safety parameter is coupled to sensor geometry. A field size isn't just about stopping distance; it's also about what the sensor can still see at that distance. Write the coupling down as code, not as a remembered number.
  • Regression-test safety after every change to the safety path, even an "obvious improvement". The unit tests checked the formula; only the course checked the robot.
  • Shared resources need locks, even on a single developer machine. Especially when the developer is an agent running things in the background.

docs.title: Seven decisions, and the cheapest hedgehog protection there is
docs.text: We reviewed the Phase 5 (perception) plan together and made all seven decisions in it. Then we built the first piece, which needs no camera and no AI: the robot doesn't mow in the dark.

docs.title: The decisions
docs.text:
# Question Decided D1 Can the AI overrule the lidar? No. Chris: "the lidar is and should be treated as always 'more confidently true' than an AI interpretation of data." The lidar wins on is something there; the AI may only add caution; a degraded lidar is a fault, never the camera's turn D2 Low animals in long grass The robot won't mow grass taller than ~8 cm by default (so the lidar can still tell a hedgehog from the lawn). An app switch overrides it, for one mow only D3 Detector licence Apache-2.0 for now; the detector is a plug-in, so anyone can swap in another model later without re-licensing the rest D4 Camera privacy Images never leave the robot; recordings exclude the camera (a test enforces it, today); everything beyond the lawn boundary is masked D5 People and pets Full stop and wait, not "blade off and carry on". Chris: "better not even bump into anyone." Dog mess: tell the owner, with an app option to avoid the spot until it's cleaned up D6 When is it good enough to mow unattended? Not decided yet, on purpose: no numbers until there's a baseline from real images D7 Order Deterministic work first (night rule, grass, lidar health, moving people), the camera after

A pattern emerged: every setting defaults to the safer choice. Loosening one is app-only (never the buttons), needs a confirmation, and expires on its own.

docs.title: The night rule
docs.text:
Hedgehogs, toads and foxes come out at dusk, which is when robot mowers hurt them. So: no mowing from 30 minutes before sunset to 30 minutes after sunrise, computed from the robot's own GNSS position and the date with the NOAA solar equations. No internet, no time-zone database, no override.

The unit tests check it against published sunrise and sunset tables (Philadelphia in June and December, Greenwich, and Tromsø's midnight sun and polar night). One test is there because of a trap: at a western longitude a summer evening is already tomorrow in UTC, so asking "when is sunrise on today's UTC date?" at 19:30 local returns tomorrow's sunrise and refuses to mow in broad daylight. The first version of that test passed even with the bug in place, because it checked a moment that was night under either reading. So the test was rewritten, and then checked by putting the bug back in and watching it fail.

The simulator's clock starts at zero, so each run says what UTC time sim time zero is (default: 10:00 local, midsummer). Two runs, judged by a report that recomputes "is mowing allowed?" for every blade command in the bag, independently of the mission's own bookkeeping:

Run Scenario Result night-dusk-2 Mowing at 19:57 local; the cutoff is 20:02:18 Rule switched at 20:02:18, sent home 1 s later, docked 26 s later, stayed on the dock. Blade on after the cutoff: 0.9 s night-dawn-1 On the dock at 05:57; mowing allowed from 06:01:25 Waited, then started at 06:01:26; finished the patch (97.3% coverage)

One bug on the way: the first dusk run never started. Launch arguments are YAML, and YAML reads 2026-06-21T23:57:00Z as a date object, which ROS parameters refuse. It's the same family as the bug from Phase 1, where 60 was read as an integer. The value is now forced to a string, and the quirk is written down.

Next: real grass in the simulator. The lawn has been a flat plane all along, and a flat lawn flatters the lidar.

docs.title: The website gets a front door (and a budget)
docs.text: Chris's feedback on the public site: the styling and tone are right, but it's very tech-forward. The first thing a visitor met was a canvas of stripes labelled "RTK FIXED" and "300 rad/s". Good if you already care, but no help if you don't. So the site now has two layers: a plain-language front page that says what Fauerbot is for, what the goals are and what they cost, and all the detail one click behind it on How it works.

docs.title: A crowdfunding page with nothing to sell
docs.text:
The shape we borrowed is a crowdfunding campaign page: a promise at the top, a status panel, goals, where the money goes, risks, an FAQ. It's a good shape because it answers the questions people actually have, in the order they have them. But we're not raising money, so every part had to be honest about that:

  • The status panel shows the budget to a real robot (≈ $2,500), then $0 raised, and says why: the founder is paying, and we're not asking. A "1 of 5 goals" meter replaces the usual funding bar.
  • The goals are the hardware stages H1 to H4 from the plan, renamed for people who don't read plans: sensors on a garden cart, a real robot with the blade off, eyes for safety, blade on and supervised. Each has a cost and a status. The custom chrome body is a stretch goal, because that's what it is.
  • The budget has a source for every price: our parts list (checked 8 Nov), used YardForce Classic 500 listings at about €300 (≈ $340), the OpenMower board kit at €225–300 (≈ $250–340), and the Livox Mid-360 3D lidar at its $979 list price. The lidar is the biggest single item. The safety electronics (about $100) are the only estimate, and the table says so.
  • "And to make one you could buy?" gets an honest non-answer. Certification, moulds and insurance are a different scale of money, and any number we put there today would be a guess.
  • Risks and challenges opens with the blade, because that is the real risk.

The "how to help" section asks for attention, not money: follow along, share it. The ideas for later (a course and a blade-free kit for builders) are listed as ideas, with no prices, so nobody reads them as a pre-order.

docs.title: Moving the detail, not deleting it
docs.text:
Nothing technical was removed. The old landing page moved to how-it-works.html almost word for word: the findings, the mowing numbers, the stage list, the diagrams, the parts list and the safety interlock. The only changes there are a link back and an updated licence note (Apache-2.0 and CERN-OHL-S are decided now). The front page keeps the animated lawn, with plainer labels, and ends with the latest devlog posts.

Two small bugs turned up in the screenshots. The "All 20 posts" button had rendered as "All20posts" for weeks: a flex container drops the spaces between a text run and a <span>. On a phone, the budget table scrolled its cost column off the screen, and the cost is the whole point of that table. It now stacks on narrow screens. scripts/website_screenshot.py now shoots both pages at both sizes and reports any horizontal overflow (none).

docs.title: Real hosting
docs.text: The site is also on real hosting now, on GitHub Pages from a separate public repository that holds only the generated files. make publish-site builds the site and pushes it there. The source stays private for now.

docs.title: Blade off on the paving
docs.text: A spinning blade on gravel or paving throws stones. Until now the robot avoided the problem by never leaving the lawn, so it couldn't cross a garden path, a patio or a driveway at all. That's the first of the three ground hazards in the perception plan (5.1c). The other two are drop-offs and slopes.

docs.title: The rule
docs.text:
The lawn map gets a new kind of area, path: a hard surface the robot may drive over. The rule is one sentence:

The blade may only spin while every blade disc is on a lawn and off every path.

Each disc is grown by 5 cm to allow for position error, since RTK GNSS is good to a few centimetres, not to zero. Where the robot will turn on the spot, the check uses the whole circle the blades sweep round the turn. That matters for Tachyon, whose two blades sit out to the sides.

docs.title: Crossing a path
docs.text:
The robot already knows its route, so it looks a metre ahead along it for the first spot where the rule would fail:

  1. Half a metre out it slows down. For the last 20 cm it creeps at docking speed.
  2. It stops when a blade's edge (plus the 5 cm) is 3 cm from the paving.
  3. It waits 2 seconds with the blade off. The simulated blade stops in under one; the real motor must brake to a stop within two, which is already a build-plan test.
  4. It crosses with the blade stopped.
  5. On the far side, once every disc is back on grass, it stops again and soft-starts the blade (the same 3 s ramp as at the start of a mow), then mows on.

Changing blade speed while standing still means the grass right up to the paving gets cut on both sides. The robot also checks its actual position as well as its planned one, so a robot running a few centimetres off its line stops just as early.

docs.title: The test
docs.text:
The simulated yard has a new 5 × 5 m Path patch with a 0.8 m paved garden path straight across it. The stripes run across the path, so every one of them crosses it: the worst case.

Robot Blade spinning over the path Closest a spinning blade came Coverage of what it can reach Crossings, time cost Ion never 3.4 cm 96.3% 16, 132 s Tachyon (twin blades) never 2.2 cm 97.4% 10, 81 s

Runs hard-4-ion and hard-4-tachyon, measured from ground truth at 10 Hz. "Spinning" means faster than 5 rad/s.

The first try got the safety part right but stopped about 10 cm short of the path, which left a 15 cm strip uncut on each side. Creeping the last 20 cm fixed that. The next try had a real bug: the look-ahead checked the route every 5 cm, so a 3 cm stopping distance only fired once the robot was already inside the margin, and Tachyon's blade stopped 0.1 cm from the paving. The blade never touched it, but that was luck, not margin. The look-ahead now narrows down the exact stopping point, and the closest approach is a few centimetres: the 5 cm margin minus roughly the position error, as intended.

There's still a strip along each edge of the path that a round blade can't reach without going over it, much like the strip along a fence. The coverage report now defines "what the plan can reach" as what the blade can cut under the rule, and shows the rest as trimmer territory.

docs.title: What's not good yet
docs.text:
• Crossings are slow. 132 seconds of a six-minute mow is stopping, waiting and restarting. The planner should mow each side of a path on its own and cross once, or stripe along the path instead of across it. It doesn't yet.
  • This trusts the map. If a path isn't drawn, or is drawn in the wrong place, the robot mows straight over it. The next step is the second layer: paving is flat in a way grass isn't, and the lidar already measures grass height. A lane of returns under a centimetre, tight on the ground plane, isn't grass, so the blade goes off even if the map is wrong.
  • The paving is only a picture. In the simulator, the path is flat paint on the ground, not gravel. Real gravel will look different to the lidar, which is why the sensing layer needs testing on real ground.

docs.title: Off the dock and back on, for every platform
docs.text: The first full smoke test of the six platforms had two failures, both at the dock: Tachyon never left it, and Vector mowed the patch and then missed the dock three times. Neither was about the dock. One was a clock, one was steering, and fixing them turned up a third problem that isn't finished.

docs.title: Tachyon: the robot that was "stuck" for 1 millisecond
docs.text:
Tachyon aborted with "no progress in LEAVE (blocked by the safety gate?)", one millisecond after starting to leave, with no safety stops at all. The mission had been planning: Tachyon's plan for the 5 × 4 m smoke patch took 44 seconds. The mission node runs on one thread, so while it planned, its copy of the simulator's clock didn't move. When planning finished, the clock jumped 44 seconds at once, and the very next check saw "no progress for more than 30 s" and gave up.

Two fixes:

  • A stall in our own loop is not the robot being stuck. If the mission's loop sees the clock jump more than 2 s between two ticks, it moves the progress timer by the same amount. The robot was never asked to move in that time.
  • Planning is 3 to 7 times faster for the big robots. Almost all the time went into one question, asked about 100,000 times: does the body's swept area stay inside the lawn? The planner built that area as a union of every pose, then tested it. But a union is inside an area exactly when every piece is, so it now tests the pieces and stops at the first one outside. The plans are identical, checked for all six robots on every lawn; Vector's back yard went from 36 s to 5 s, Tachyon's smoke patch from 33 s to 12 s. That still isn't fast, and a Raspberry Pi will be slower than this PC, so it's on the list.

docs.title: Vector: weaving onto the dock
docs.text:
Vector reached the dock each time within 1 cm, but turned 13.6° off the dock's axis; the contacts allow 8°. On the last metre its heading swung from +22° to −18°. A four-wheel skid-steer turns harder when it's rolling than when it pivots: rolling, its tyres scrub less, so the same wheel-speed difference turns it about 25% more. With the docking follower looking only 0.3 m ahead, that extra gain was enough to make it weave.

The docking lookahead is now a per-platform setting in the robot's profile, like its scrub factor: Ion keeps its tuned 0.3 m, Vector uses 0.6 m. Next run, Vector docked first time, 2° off.

docs.title: Vector: overshooting corners, and a heading it can't trust
docs.text:
With docking fixed, Vector still failed one check: at one stripe end its path ran 19.6 cm wide of the plan (the limit is 15 cm). Told to pivot at 1.0 rad/s, it spun at 1.29, set off 45° wrong and had to pivot again. Its pivot rate is now a profile setting too: 0.6 rad/s for Vector, Ion's 1.0 unchanged. That brought the worst error down to 16 cm.

The rest is in its position estimate. On straights, Vector's heading estimate wanders by up to 5° while its gyro matches the truth exactly. The culprit is the global filter, which also fuses RTK positions:

Vector run Heading error, global (wheels + gyro + RTK) Heading error, local (wheels + gyro) smoke-6: as before 3.14° 0.28° smoke-7: yaw from the gyro only 2.79° 0.26° smoke-8: trust the wheels' speed less 2.84° 0.55°

The local filter's heading is fine, so the gyro is fine. A skid-steer slides sideways when it turns while rolling (up to 0.12 m/s in the simulator), so its wheels' idea of where it went drifts 20 to 26 cm over a run, against Ion's 5. Each RTK fix then corrects that drift, and the global filter puts part of the correction into the heading. Taking yaw from the gyro alone (the usual practice for skid-steer and tracks) helped a little and stays, as the default for those drives. Trusting the wheels' speed less didn't help, so it was reverted. A proper fix means tuning Vector's filter, or modelling the slide, and that's the next job for Vector.

docs.title: The smoke tests now
docs.text:
Robot smoke-4 smoke-9 Reachable coverage Turn calibration Heading error (global) Ion PASS PASS 99.3% 1.00 1.29° Quark PASS PASS 98.7% 1.00 1.26° Photon PASS PASS 99.2% 1.00 1.19° Vector FAIL: missed the dock 3 times FAIL: docks first time; 17.9 cm off at one stripe end 98.7% 1.03 3.07° Graviton PASS PASS 99.2% 1.11 1.11° Tachyon FAIL: never left the dock PASS 99.9% 1.00 1.10°

Five of six pass, and every platform now undocks, mows and docks. Graviton also takes its yaw from the gyro alone now, and its heading error fell slightly (1.17° to 1.11°). The battle cards on the Platforms page show these results.

docs.title: What this doesn't prove
docs.text: The sliding is the simulator's idea of rubber on grass: a real Vector may slide more or less. The settings that fixed it (lookahead, pivot rate) are tuned in simulation and will need re-tuning on a real robot, which is why they live in the profile rather than in the code.

docs.title: Dollars, a feed, and who makes the board
docs.text: Chris read the new front page and asked three things. Some prices looked like pounds. Could the devlog have an RSS feed? And are we building on the OpenMower board, or designing our own?

docs.title: Prices in dollars
docs.text:
They were euros, not pounds: the RTK receiver, the used YardForce mower and the OpenMower kit are priced by European sellers. The site now shows everything in US dollars, rounded, at an approximate $1.12 per € (the November 2026 rate), and says so beside each table. The parts list in the repo keeps the seller's own price and adds the dollar figure next to it, because that's the number you'll actually pay at checkout.

Converting moved two estimates. The first real-robot goal is now ≈ $600–700, and the sensor stage is ≈ $500–700. The total for goals 2–5 is unchanged at ≈ $2,200–2,500.

docs.title: An RSS feed
docs.text: The devlog now has a feed: feed_rss_created.xml. It's linked from the front page, the site footer, and the RSS icon at the bottom of every devlog page, and feed readers will find it on their own. The dates come from each post rather than from git, because the blog is built in a container that doesn't have the repo's history.

docs.title: The board: buy one first, then make our own
docs.text:
The board sits between the Pi and the mower: it drives the three motors, reads the lift, tilt and stop sensors, charges the battery, and holds the hardware blade interlock. Our software talks to it through one ROS 2 node, so whichever board we use, nothing above that node changes.

OpenMower has two hardware generations:

  • v1 is a single board. A web shop sells it complete for about $340.
  • v2, the current one, is a carrier board for each mower model with two plug-in modules: the microcontroller and the motor controllers. The project's own seller sells the kit, through the OpenMower community.

Either is a good place to start. We'd take v1 from the shop if two things hold:

  • It's in stock.
  • It isn't a dead end. It isn't: the OpenMower project still maintains it (its September 2026 release fixed a v1 board setting). For us it matters even less, because our software talks to the board through our own node. Moving to v2 or to our own board later changes that node and nothing else.

One thing to check before buying: that the kit fits the revision of the used mower we find. If v1 is out of stock or doesn't fit, we buy v2.

Then comes the longer-term plan: design and build our own board. The kit on the bench teaches us the mower's wiring and its real motors, and gives our driver node a known-good board to test against. Then we design ours next to it:

  • The reference: OpenMower publishes its YardForce carrier under CC BY 4.0, so its schematic is the reference for everything the mower plugs into. We can reuse it with credit, even in a board we might one day sell.
  • What ours adds: the hardware blade interlock and a separate safety microcontroller.
  • Parts: ones anyone can buy.

The full comparison, with licences, is in hardware/controller-options.md. None of this is urgent: the next hardware stage is a push-cart with no motors at all.

docs.title: Grass is not an obstacle (it took nine stops to get there)
docs.text: Until tonight the sim lawn was a flat green plane. Real grass is 5 to 10 cm tall, and our 3D-lidar safety gate stopped for anything 3 cm above the ground. So we grew grass the lidar can see, and the robot never left the dock. Seventeen runs later it mows a whole zone in 7 cm grass, over bumps and a 25 cm mound, with zero false stops. Every fix in between came from a stop the robot explained itself.

docs.title: Growing grass a lidar can see
docs.text:
Gazebo's gpu_lidar renders the scene, so it sees visual geometry. A green texture is invisible to it. Grass has to be geometry: 58,000 tufts, each a thin four-sided pyramid, on a jittered 7 cm grid with heights of nominal ±25%. They're all one OBJ mesh with no collision (the robot drives through grass), so the GPU draws one thing, not 58,000 models. It takes 0.2 s to generate and is 12 MB. make mow-run GRASS=0.07.

For uneven ground, TERRAIN=bumpy adds a collision mesh: twelve 3–6 cm bumps and one broad 25 cm mound, with slopes up to 12°. Heights are never below zero, so the old plane still holds up the rest of the yard, and the dock stays level. (First try: Gazebo segfaulted. DART needs a normal per vertex in a collision mesh. Without them it drops the mesh and the server crashes. We now compute them from the terrain's gradient.)

docs.title: The baseline: stuck at the dock
docs.text:
Run What Result grass-3d-1 7 cm grass, the gate as it was STOP at 0.35 m before leaving the dock, latched forever. 0 m² mowed

That's the honest starting point. "Obstacle = anything 3 cm above z = 0" makes every blade an obstacle.

docs.title: The stops, one at a time
docs.text:
The 3D point cloud is too heavy to record, so after the first failure the gate started keeping evidence: every STOP event now carries the nearest offending points (position and height above the ground) and the fitted ground plane. scripts/stop_probe.py <run> turns that into world coordinates. Each row below is one stop it explained:

Run The stop What it really was Fix grass-3d-2/3 0.56 m ahead while turning The flowerbed (15 cm), real, but 1 m away during a pivot Protect what the motion sweeps: a pivot checks a circle (0.575 m + 0.10 m), not a corridor grass-3d-4 0.21 m from the axle The robot itself: the lidar sees its own deck Ignore points inside the footprint grass-3d-6 one point, 10.1 cm, behind A tall tuft against a plane fitted ahead and extrapolated behind An object needs 3 returns within 10 cm; clearance = tallest grass + 3 cm = 12 cm grass-3d-7 flowerbed edge, twice Real: 13–15 cm, exactly the bed's height None in software (a decision for Chris, below) grass-bumpy-2 grass behind, 12–14 cm The forward plane was 4 cm low behind the robot A second plane fitted around the robot for pivots grass-bumpy-3 grass on a bump, 12–14 cm A plane can't follow a 6 cm bump 0.5 m wide Local ground: per-cell lowest return, capped at 4 cm above its neighbours

The cap in the last row is the important design choice. Taking each cell's lowest return as "ground" follows bumps, but a box that fills a cell completely shows only its top, and its top would become the ground. Capping a cell at its neighbours' ground + 4 cm means an object loses at most 4 cm of apparent height. A 20 cm box still reads ≥ 16 cm (a unit test checks it), and the face nearest the robot always has real ground beside it.

docs.title: Two passes
docs.text:
Run Ground Mowed False stops Coverage Cross-track max grass-open-1 flat, 7 cm grass 37.1 m² 0 98.3% 9.7 cm grass-bumpy-4 bumps + 25 cm mound, 7 cm grass 37.0 m² 0 96.3% 11.1 cm

And the 2D lidar on the same bumpy lawn (grass-bumpy-2d-1)? We expected the mound to look like a wall to a horizontal beam 15 cm up. It didn't stop the robot, but it slowed it for 124 s of a 397 s mission (the 3D gate: 5 s of 342 s). The beam meets the rising slope 1 to 1.5 m ahead, inside the slow field but outside the stop field, and once the robot is on the slope it tilts with it and the beam clears. A steeper or shorter rise would stop it. The 2D lidar was never going to see a hedgehog anyway; this is one more reason the 3D lidar is the safety sensor.

Both ran in a new lawn zone, the Open patch, between the house and the tree, with nothing raised in it. The test patch has the flowerbed, and that turned out to be its own problem.

docs.title: Still stopping for every real thing?
docs.text:
Ignoring grass is only worth something if the gate still stops for everything else. So we ran the obstacle course twice with the new gate, 3D lidar. First as a regression on the flat lawn (default clearance 3 cm), then in 7 cm grass with the 12 cm clearance:

Obstacle Height Flat, new gate 7 cm grass, clearance 12 cm pole 1 m PASS, seen at 1.47 m, 0.57 m to spare PASS, seen at 1.46 m, 0.57 m to spare box 20 cm PASS, 1.49 m, 0.58 m PASS, 1.47 m, 0.57 m child (lying) 25 cm PASS, 1.48 m, 0.57 m PASS, 1.49 m, 0.57 m ball 20 cm PASS, 1.48 m, 0.57 m PASS, 1.43 m, 0.56 m hedgehog 10 cm PASS, 1.48 m, 0.57 m HIT, never seen hose 4 cm PASS, 1.27 m, 0.56 m HIT, never seen nothing no false stops no false stops

The two hits are the result Phase 5's plan predicted, and they're why the plan has more steps. Height is the only thing the lidar measures. If the grass is 9 cm tall and a hedgehog is 10 cm tall, no threshold separates them: a clearance low enough to see the hedgehog stops for the grass. The hose lies under the grass. Two things follow. D2, the long-grass rule: keep the lawn short enough (≤ ~8 cm) that the clearance stays low. And the camera (5.3), which can tell an animal from a tuft by what it looks like, not how tall it is.

So how short is short enough? With our clearance rule (tallest grass, nominal × 1.25, plus 3 cm), a 10 cm hedgehog stays above the clearance only while the grass is under about 5.6 cm. We tested the edge: 5 cm grass, clearance 9.25 cm.

Run Result course-grass5-hedgehog-3d PASS: hedgehog seen at 1.22 m, stopped with 0.56 m to spare course-grass5-none-3d no false stops grass5-bumpy-1 (full mow, bumpy) 37.1 m², 0 false stops, coverage 96.6%

That gives D2 its number. We had pencilled in "about 8 cm", which is too tall. For the lidar alone to protect a hedgehog, the long-grass rule has to trip at about 5.5 cm of uncut grass. Our sim lawn's cut height is 6 cm, so even a fresh cut sits at the edge. That's a decision for Chris (cut lower, or accept that the camera does this job in grass over 5.5 cm).

(The flat child run needed a rerun: Gazebo started but never published /clock, a flaky start we've seen once before, unrelated to the gate.)

docs.title: A decision for Chris: raised flowerbeds
docs.text:
The 3D lidar sees a 15 cm raised bed as what it is, an obstacle. The 2D lidar never did, because it sits at 15 cm. The planner ends stripes with the nose 0.26 m from a keep-out. But since course-b the gate keeps a floor under its stop field (the blind range of the downward beams, so a hedgehog can't vanish under them), which stops the robot about 0.6 m from anything taller than the clearance. Head-on to a raised bed, those two can't both be satisfied.

  • A. The planner keeps ~0.7 m from raised keep-outs. Safe, and leaves a strip for the trimmer.
  • B. The gate ignores returns inside a mapped keep-out. Full coverage, but less caution (a child in the bed).
  • C. A by default, B as an app-only owner switch.

Claude's recommendation is A now. Nothing is built until Chris decides.

docs.title: What we learned
docs.text:
• Make the robot explain its stops. Every fix tonight came from evidence the gate logged itself. Without it we would have tuned the clearance up until the stops went away, and hidden the flowerbed problem.
  • Protect the space the motion sweeps. A stop field is about where the robot is going: a corridor when driving, a circle when turning. The old gate checked a corridor during pivots.
  • Fit the ground where you're about to measure. A plane fitted ahead was wrong behind; a plane was wrong on a bump. Each is fine for its own job.
  • One return is not an object. Real things return many points; noise and grass tips return one.

Next: 5.1a, the long-grass rule. The mowed stripe beside the robot is a free measurement of cut height, and the uncut grass ahead tells us how tall the lawn is. The clearance should come from that measurement, not from a number we typed.

docs.title: Corners: stop short, turn, merge
docs.text: The first back-yard mow with the 3D lidar (backyard-raised-2) ended against the fence. On the outer lap, 35 cm from the lawn's edge, the robot drove right up to each corner before turning. That put its nose 14 cm past the edge, and at the fence the safety gate saw the fence inside its stop field and stopped the robot for good, 0.36 m away. Against a wall it would simply have hit it.

docs.title: Why the corner was wrong
docs.text: A lap is a line the robot's axle follows. The planner offset it from the edge by half the body's width plus 5 cm, which is right for driving along an edge. At a corner the robot drives towards the next edge, and the nose sticks out 49 cm ahead of the axle. Stripes already knew this: they end 75 cm from the edge (nose plus 26 cm of reach). The lap didn't.

docs.title: The new corner
docs.text:
Where a sharp turn would put the body or the nose's reach outside the lawn, the planner now:

  1. stops short of the corner, where the nose's reach is still inside the lawn, as at a stripe end;
  2. turns in place to face along the next side;
  3. eases out onto the next side with a half-cosine blend over 1 to 3 m, so it leaves the stop straight and joins the lap straight.

The corner's tip is left for the inner lap and the trimmer. Transits that join the lap also had a problem: a full turn in place on the outer lap swung the body 22 cm outside. Now each lap gets a lead-in and a lead-out, so the robot turns where a full turn fits and eases onto the lap from there.

A new test checks the body itself, not hand-worked offsets. It drives the robot's footprint along every plan, turning in place at each vertex as the mission does, on a rectangle, an L, a triangle, a rotated rectangle and a lawn with a bed. The body must stay within 1 cm of the lawn.

docs.title: Back in the simulator
docs.text:
Run Zone Reachable coverage Body > 10 cm off the lawn Safety stops Ended backyard-raised-2 (before) Back yard, 3D lidar stopped at the fence yes, at every corner 1, permanent stuck backyard-corners-1 (after) Back yard, 3D lidar, 4 cm grass 99.2% 0 0 docked raised-6-margin (after) Test patch, raised-bed margin 96.4% 0 0 docked

The back yard took 36 minutes of sim time, 766 m of mowing, and never came within the gate's stop field of anything.

What's next

The same test, run for other robot bodies, found three more ways a corner can go wrong. That's the next post.

docs.title: Paving the map forgot
docs.text: The last post taught the robot to stop its blade before a garden path, as long as the path was on the map. If a path isn't drawn, or is drawn in the wrong place, the robot would mow straight over it. This post adds the second layer: the robot sees the paving for itself.

docs.title: What paving looks like to a lidar
docs.text:
The lidar already measures grass height to decide whether the lawn is too long to mow. Grass is 4 to 10 cm of thin blades. Paving is flat. So the safety software looks at a strip of ground just ahead of the robot, split into 20 cm squares. A square gets flagged as bare when the lidar has hit it at least four times and none of those hits is more than 2.5 cm above the ground.

One flag isn't enough. The robot keeps a map of what it has seen, in 10 cm squares. A square counts as paving once it has been flagged three times and three of its neighbours have too, because paving is an area, not a speck. Then the blade rule from the last post treats the sensed paving exactly like mapped paving: slow down, stop, cross with the blade off, restart on the far side.

docs.title: The test
docs.text:
The same 5 × 5 m patch with a paved path across it, but the robot gets a map with the path deleted. The coverage report still knows where the path really is, so it can tell whether the blade ever spun over it.

Map only (last post) Sensing only (path not mapped) Both Blade spinning over the path never never never Closest a spinning blade came 3.4 cm 9.1 cm 4.8 cm Coverage of what it can reach 96.3% 92.8% 94.6%

Runs hard-4-ion, hard-14-unmapped and hard-17-mapped, Ion, measured from ground truth at 10 Hz. The run on plain grass with no paving (hard-15-grass) found no paving at all and took the same time as before.

docs.title: Four things that went wrong first
docs.text:
The robot skipped half a stripe. This one had nothing to do with paving. Its route ran along one side of the patch, then turned round and came straight back 7.6 cm away. Running 4 cm off its line, the robot was as close to the return leg as to the leg it was on, so its idea of "how far along the route am I" jumped round the turn. It turned back 1.3 m early. Now it can't count itself round a sharp corner until it has actually reached it.

Grass looked like paving. The first sensing runs found 130 bare squares on plain grass. Every one was first seen 1.7 to 1.9 m ahead. That far out, the lidar's beams hit the lawn at a shallow angle and slip between the grass blades to the soil. Looking only 1.6 m ahead brought that to zero.

Then the blade reached the paving. With the shorter view, the robot came out of a turn 1.6 m from the path at full speed and confirmed the near edge only 0.67 m away. Too late: the blade spun over the paving 22 times in 10 Hz samples. The fix is to be careful before being sure: as soon as anything bare is in view, the robot slows to a crawl until it knows. It costs about 40 seconds on this patch, and nothing on plain grass.

Two layers stopped too early. With the map and the sensing both on, the robot stopped 10 cm short of the path instead of 3 cm, because the sensed edge lands about 5 cm past the real one. Next to a mapped path the map now wins: sensed paving within 6 cm of it is ignored. That still catches paving drawn more than 6 cm out of place, and within that, the 5 cm blade margin covers it.

docs.title: What's not good yet
docs.text:
• 94.6% with both layers is just under our 95% bar. About one row in six, the sensed edge lands 15 cm out instead of 5. The 20 cm squares are too coarse to find an edge precisely. Smaller squares should fix it; that's on the list.
  • It can't see paving right under its nose. The view starts 0.6 m ahead, so if a turn ends closer to the paving than that, only the map can stop the blade.
  • It's still simulated paving. Flat paint on the simulated ground, not real gravel. Real gravel is lumpy, wet paving shines, and both will look different to the lidar, so this needs testing on real ground. Later, the camera can help tell paving, gravel and grass apart.

Next: drop-offs, the worst of the three ground hazards.

docs.title: Raised beds: a margin, a switch, and a flowerbed mistaken for long grass
docs.text:
The sim's flowerbed is a 15 cm raised box. To the 3D lidar, its edge is an obstacle like any other, and the safety gate never lets the robot's nose get closer than about 0.57 m to an obstacle (the lidar's blind range for a 4 cm object, plus 10 cm). The planner ended stripes 0.26 m from keep-outs. Those two numbers can't both hold, so we decided on option C: by default the robot keeps further from raised keep-outs and leaves the strip for the trimmer, and an owner switch lets it mow right up to them.

Building it turned up three more bugs. A raised bed can pass for long grass, and so can a fence. And the robot's route home could take it into a corner it couldn't get out of.

docs.title: The baseline: three failures in one run
docs.text:
Before changing anything we mowed the Test patch with the 3D lidar, in 4 cm grass (raised-1-baseline). It lasted 167 seconds:

  1. Rounding the bed's corner, the gate stopped with the bed 0.55 m ahead. That was expected.
  2. One second later the long-grass rule tripped: "uncut grass 15.5 cm > 5.5 cm". The robot went home and declared the lawn overdue.
  3. The grass clearance had ratcheted to its 10 cm cap. Of the three, this is the one that matters.

The second and third come from the same cause. The grass measurement takes the median of the tallest return in each 20 cm cell of the lane ahead. At the corner, the bed's edge ran diagonally across the lane and filled most of its cells, so the median was the bed. The clearance follows the tallest grass measured this mission, and it never comes down (a ratchet, for reasons in the long-grass post). So one look at a flowerbed raised the obstacle threshold for the rest of the mission, and that threshold is the margin that keeps a hedgehog visible.

Reproducing this in a unit test took two tries. A bed square-on and filling the view reads as ground: the per-cell ground correction holds each cell to its neighbours' level, so only cells near an edge stand out. Placed at 45°, as it was at the corner, it reads 14–15 cm. The test uses the 45° bed.

docs.title: Option C
docs.text:
The lawn model gets a flag: a keep-out can be "raised": true (the flowerbed, and the tree, whose trunk the lidar sees too). Then:

  • Never grass. The safety gate loads the map, takes the robot's pose, and leaves every return inside a mapped raised keep-out (plus 10 cm) out of the grass measurement. This applies whatever the switch says, because a flowerbed is never grass. It also leaves those returns out of the ground fit, since a bed isn't ground either.
  • The margin (default). The planner grows raised keep-outs by 0.45 m before planning. Every lap, stripe end and route then keeps the extra distance: the nose ends stripes 0.71 m from the bed, outside the gate's 0.57 m.
  • The switch. mow_up_to_raised drops the margin, and the gate then ignores returns inside the mapped bed as obstacles too. Anything outside it still counts, including an animal pressed against the bed's edge. A unit test maps the bed 1 m too far away and checks that the unmapped part stops the robot again. The switch is logged at mission start, like the long-grass switch. On the real robot it will be app-only.

docs.title: The route home that went the long way
docs.text:
The first runs with option C mowed perfectly, then failed on the way home: "no progress in RETURN". Both stopped at the same spot, (8.9, −7.0), in the lawn's far corner, facing a fence 0.56 m away.

The route home had gone 19.3 m east into that corner instead of 11.1 m round the bed. Routes come from a visibility graph: nodes on the edge of the free area, joined wherever the straight line between them stays inside it. Two nodes on a keep-out's rounded buffer are joined by a chord, and a chord across a curve cuts into the buffer. So every link round the bed was rejected, and the shortest route left ran along the fence. The bigger raised margin made the curve bigger, which is how we found it, but the bug didn't need the margin: the switch-on run, with no margin, got stuck in the same corner.

The fix is to put the nodes 6 cm inside the free area. Simplification moves them by at most 5 cm, so they stay inside, and the chords between them do too. A regression test plans that same route home.

docs.title: The fence that was long grass
docs.text:
Because the route fix changes every route, we ran a full back-yard mow as a regression check. It lasted 263 seconds. Heading north near the fence, the lane read 29.7 cm of uncut grass, and the long-grass rule sent the robot home.

This one has nothing to do with raised beds. Returns above 30 cm were dropped as "not grass", but only the returns: the bottom 30 cm of a fence or a hedge stayed, and topped every cell it was in. It hadn't shown up before because this was the first back-yard run with the 3D lidar in grass since the long-grass rule went in. Two fixes, one per layer:

  • Map: grass is only measured on the mapped lawn. A fence, a wall or a patio past the lawn's edge is never grass.
  • Sensing: a 20 cm cell with anything above 30 cm in it is an object, and is dropped whole.

A low wall under 30 cm that isn't on the map would still fool it: the map is what covers that case.

The rerun (backyard-raised-2) had no long-grass trips. It still failed, and the reason was older than anything in this post. The outer lap runs 0.35 m inside the lawn's edge, so at a corner the robot drives straight at the edge and its nose, 0.49 m ahead of the axle, ends up 14 cm past it. In the sim the fence stands 0.5 m beyond the lawn's edge, so the nose was 0.36 m from the fence, inside the 3D lidar's 0.57 m stop field. The robot stopped there and never moved again. The back yard had never been mowed with the 3D lidar before, so nothing had shown it. On a real lawn that ends at a wall, the same corner would put the nose into the wall. That gets fixed next.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
make raised-test mows the Test patch twice. analysis/raised_keepout_report.py judges each run:

Check Margin (default) Switch on Mission done, docked done, docked Safety stops near a raised keep-out 0 0 Long-grass trips 0 0 Grass clearance while mowing (cap 10 cm) 9.8 cm 9.5 cm Blade edge's closest approach to the bed 0.57 m (≥ 0.45) 0.16 m (≤ 0.30) Reachable area cut 95.5% 96.8% Whole lawn cut 63.2% 80.5%

The last row is the price of the default. With the margin, about 0.6 m round the bed stays uncut: 5.6 m² more for the trimmer on this small patch. We think that's the right default for now, because it doesn't ask the robot to trust its map near a solid object. The switch is there for an owner who has checked the bed is mapped well.

docs.title: Smaller things
docs.text:
• The tests interfered with each other. The battery integration test failed in the full suite and passed alone. colcon runs packages' tests in parallel on one ROS network, and the new gate tests published config events that the battery test counted. make test now runs packages one at a time: 124 tests, about 20 seconds.
  • The website's diagram tabs did nothing (Chris, on a phone). display: grid on the panels beat the browser's own [hidden] rule, so all five diagrams always showed. Fixed. On phones each diagram also opens full size.

docs.title: Next: corners, then ground hazards
docs.text: First, lap corners. A lawn's edge can be a wall, so the outer lap has to turn before the nose reaches it. Then ground hazards. Chris raised three more ways to get hurt without hitting anything: falling off a step or wall, a slope too steep, and a spinning blade over a driveway. Each gets a map layer and an independent sensing layer. The lidar can see missing or sunken ground ahead, the slope ahead, and a surface too flat to be grass. The plan is in docs/phase5-perception.md, section 5.1c. Hard surfaces come first.

docs.title: Six robots, one brain
docs.text: Chris: "I bet I will come up with a few different hardware platforms. Two-wheel drive, four-wheel drive, tank drive, taller, shorter, wider." A review of the code found the robot's size written out in at least six places, two wheel joints hard-coded, sensing windows sized for one body, one blade assumed everywhere, and no way to tell the simulator which robot to run. So we fixed all of it the practical way: by designing five more robots and making the whole stack run each of them.

docs.title: The six
docs.text:
Drive Size (L × W × H) Cut For Ion two wheels + caster 61 × 60 × 35 cm 36 cm small and medium lawns; the one we're building first Quark two wheels + caster 46 × 42 × 27 cm 24 cm side passages and small lawns Photon Ion + 1.1 m mast + solar roof 61 × 60 × 115 cm 36 cm long grass, low hedges, no powered dock Vector four-wheel skid-steer 82 × 74 × 42 cm 46 cm rough ground, roots, molehills Graviton tracks 86 × 76 × 45 cm 46 cm slopes, soft and wet ground Tachyon two wheels + 2 casters, twin blades 95 × 100 × 40 cm 70 cm big open lawns

The names come from physics, with a future-tech feel; Chris asked for cool ones. Each one has a battle card, a 3D render, drawings, specs, a parts list and a build plan on the new Platforms page. Only Ion is being built; the other five are first-pass concepts, simulated but not built, and their prices are estimates.

docs.title: One file per robot
docs.text:
Each platform is one YAML file: the body, the drive (type, wheels per side, track width, how much it slips turning), the blades, where each sensor sits, the battery, and a design sheet. A small pure-Python module loads it and works out every number the software needs. Nothing robot-sized is written anywhere else any more:

  • the planner takes its stripe spacing, edge lap, stripe-end clearance, turning clearance, raised-bed margin and footprint from it;
  • the safety gate takes its corridor, pivot circle, ground windows and obstacle ceiling (a 1.15 m robot must see a branch at 1.3 m);
  • the power model scales rolling resistance with mass, turning scrub with the drive, blade power with cut width;
  • the simulator model is generated from it: xacro reads the YAML, so a four-wheel robot gets four drive joints and a twin-blade robot two blade motors with no new XML;
  • the reports judge each run with the robot that ran it, which every node now logs.

make mow-run ROBOT=vector runs the whole stack on Vector. For Ion, every number came out exactly as before; tests pin that.

docs.title: What the other bodies found
docs.text:
The planner's "body stays on the lawn" test, from the corner fix, now runs for every platform. It failed on its first run, in three ways:

  1. Skid-steer and tracks turn about the middle of the body, so the tail swings out as far as the nose. Ion turns about its rear axle, and its long end swings away from the edge. Vector and Graviton swung their tails 14 cm over the edge at every corner. Now, where Ion's corner doesn't fit, the robot first eases inward to where a turn does, then turns and merges back out.
  2. Tachyon's 0.80 m nose went 39 cm over while angling back out onto the lap, and 3 cm into a bed while sliding between the two laps round it. Merges can now be longer, and the slide is as long as the nose needs (Ion's stays 2 m; Tachyon's is 6 m).
  3. Where nothing fits (a side too short for the body to stop, turn and merge), the whole lap moves inward until every corner fits. The body never goes over the edge; the price is an uncut strip, which the coverage report shows. This one also caught a bug in Ion's own plans: on the Test patch, the south-west corner next to the flowerbed's margin had swung Ion's body over the zone's edge in every run. That lap now runs 5 cm further in.

Moving the whole lap is blunt: for Tachyon in the back yard, one tight corner moves it in 40 cm all the way round. Moving in only the sides next to the bad corner is on the list.

docs.title: Smoke tests, not 30-minute runs
docs.text:
Every platform needs checking whenever the code changes, and the full regression set takes hours. So each gets a smoke test instead: make smoke ROBOT=<name> undocks, mows a 5 × 4 m patch in front of the dock at full simulator speed, and docks. make smoke-all does all six. A report checks that every node agreed which robot it was, the model has the profile's joints, the mission docked, there were no false stops, and the coverage report's checks pass. It also checks turn calibration: during turns in place, the real yaw rate over what the wheel odometry believes. Skid-steer and tracks slip sideways to turn, so the odometry uses an "effective track" (track × a scrub factor). 1.0 means that guess matches how the simulated body actually slips.

Robot Reachable coverage Turn calibration Result Ion 99.1% 1.00 PASS Quark 99.2% 1.00 PASS Photon 99.3% 1.00 PASS Vector 98.0% 0.99 FAIL: mowed the patch, then failed to dock three times Graviton 99.0% 1.11 PASS Tachyon 0% none FAIL: never got off the dock

Four of six pass first time (smoke-4, about two minutes each). Graviton's tracks turn 11% faster than its odometry thinks, inside the ±25% the test allows; its scrub factor gets a nudge when there's a real one to measure. The two failures are both at the dock, not the lawn: the undocking and docking moves still assume Ion's size. That's the next post.

The first full set caught something no unit test would: Quark never left the dock. The safety gate stopped it 27 times for an "obstacle 1 cm ahead", a 30 cm-wide something 15 cm up that moved with the robot. It was Quark's own deck. Its 3D lidar sat 4 cm above the deck, so the lowest beam (−25°) skimmed the deck's front edge (−26.6°) and returned points on it, right at the nose. Ion's lidar sits level with its deck top, so the beams that hit Ion's deck do it inside the lidar's 10 cm minimum range and are dropped: lucky, not designed. Three fixes: Quark's lidar moved up 3 cm; a profile now fails validation if its lowest beam is within 5° of its own deck edge; and the gate's forward check ignores returns within 3 cm of the body, as its turning check already did.

Before any of that, make test checks each profile without a simulator: it validates, renders to a URDF that matches it, the planner keeps its body on four lawns and out of a bed, and the gate and power model follow its body.

docs.title: Battle cards
docs.text:
Chris asked for "pictures and all. Battle cards. Something cool." So the Platforms page now deals a card per robot: a 3D render, a class (Scout, Brawler, Climber...), stat bars, a special and a weakness, and the latest smoke-test result. A head-to-head picker compares any two. Each robot also has its own page, with a 3D view you can spin.

The renders are generated from the same YAML the simulator reads, not drawn: a small three.js model puts the wheels, tracks, casters, mast, solar roof and sensors where the profile says they are, and a headless browser photographs it (scripts/render_platforms.sh). The shell's shape and colours are illustration; the positions aren't. Most stats are computed too: cut width, top speed, the turning circle, the lidar's blind zone. Range, slope and cost are the design sheets' estimates, and the page says so. Making the model also caught a real bug: Tachyon's deck stuck 5 mm out of its own footprint, which a new test now checks for every robot.

docs.title: What this doesn't prove
docs.text: The simulated skid-steer and tracks are approximations: a track is three road wheels, and slip is whatever the physics engine does with rubber-ish friction. The scrub factor is a guess until a real one is measured. And smoke tests check that each body works end to end, not that it's safe: the full safety and coverage set still runs on Ion only.

docs.title: The edge of the terrace
docs.text: A mower can hurt itself, or someone near it, without hitting anything. The worst way is driving off an edge: a retaining wall, a step, a pond bank. A fall can't be undone. This post gives the robot two separate ways to stay on top: the map, and its own eyes.

docs.title: A terrace to fall off
docs.text:
The simulated yard got a new feature: a 30 cm raised terrace, 3.5 by 3 m, with walls on three sides and a 2.5 m ramp up the fourth. The lawn on top is a mowing zone like any other.

The map layer is the simple part. An edge can be marked as a drop. The robot keeps an extra 15 cm back from it, on top of its usual margin, and routes between lawns never run along it. On the correct map the robot mowed 98% of the terrace it could reach, with no false stops. The closest its body came to an edge was 19 cm.

The sensing layer is for when the map is wrong. The robot gets a map with the terrace drawn 0.5 m bigger than it really is, so the planned route runs straight off the walls. It has to notice the edge itself.

docs.title: What an edge looks like to a lidar
docs.text:
The 3D lidar looks forward and down. "Ground much lower than the wheels" sounds like the obvious test for an edge, and it was wrong. The bumpy test lawn has a 25 cm mound. From the top of it the far side is 15 to 29 cm below the wheels, just like a wall seen from the top. Replaying an old run along its route, 23 positions would have stopped for a cliff that was really a gentle hump.

What a wall has and a slope doesn't is a shadow. The lidar can't see a wall's face, so between the top and the lower ground there's a band where no laser beam lands. The robot now calls something a drop only when it sees level ground, then that gap, then ground at least 15 cm lower:

A crest casts a shadow too, but only when seen from far off, where the beam just grazes it. Up close the beams come down more steeply and the far side of a crest shows up, while a wall's face never does. So the shadow has to start within 0.9 m of the robot's nose. With those two rules, the replays found no false drops on the mound or the terrace. A real wall is spotted when the nose is 0.76 to 0.94 m from it.

Tuning this in the simulator would have meant a 5-minute run per guess. Instead there's now a small offline copy of the lidar: it casts the same 16 beams over the same terrain and matches the simulator's ground estimate to within 0.2 mm. A whole route replays in seconds.

docs.title: The test
docs.text: With the map 0.5 m too big, the robot drove up the ramp and turned onto the terrace toward the east wall, at an angle. As it turned, it saw the drop and stopped. It backed straight away from the edge by 30 cm, then gave up the mission with the reason "drop where the map says lawn". Its body never went over the real edge, but the margin was thin: its front corner stopped 12 cm from the edge. Head-on, an edge is seen with the nose 0.76 m away. A turn that swings the robot toward an edge brings it into view much closer. Giving up is deliberate: if the map is that wrong, a person should look before the robot mows there again.

docs.title: What broke on the way
docs.text:
Most of the work was in the parts that were already there, made to cope with ground at two heights.

  • The ground estimate followed the lower yard. Crossing the ramp toward its open side, most of the ground the lidar saw was the yard below. The fitted ground sank to match it, so the grass on the ramp read as a 10 cm obstacle. Now the robot tries a second fit that leaves out the ground below its own wheels, and keeps whichever fits the ground just ahead better.
  • Next to a step down, grass grew. Each patch of ground is measured against its neighbours, so a box's top isn't mistaken for the floor. Beside a step, the lower neighbour made the upper side's grass read 10 cm tall, and the robot stopped while turning on the ramp. An object's floor is visible in front of it and on both sides of it, so that is now the rule.
  • One fix too far. A cap on that height worked for obstacles. Applied to grass too, it made the grass just over the ramp's crest read as bare paving, and the blade kept stopping for paving that didn't exist (87% mowed). The cap now applies to obstacles only.
  • The wrong map was wrong in the wrong place. Drawn 0.5 m bigger all round, it also took in the low yard beside the ramp. The route started down there and ran into the ramp's side, a real 10 cm step. The robot stopped for it, correctly. Now only the three walls you could fall off are drawn too far out.
  • A ghost simulator. Several earlier test runs wouldn't start. A simulator from an old run had kept running in the background for two hours. With it gone, every run started.

The obstacle course still passes after all this: on bare ground every obstacle is seen; in 7 cm grass, everything but the garden hose, which was never seen in grass.

docs.title: Not covered yet
docs.text:
Two cases the lidar can't settle on its own. A turn that ends facing an edge already close to the nose: the first ground in view is low, with no level ground nearer to compare with, which is exactly how the mound's far side looks. And an edge running alongside the robot: looking sideways past it, the lidar again sees only low ground. The 12 cm in the test was the first case, caught in time but not by much. For now the map's margin is the answer to both. Two cheap downward distance sensors at the front corners, a hardware option still to decide, would cover them without the lidar.

Also found: coming down the mound in long grass, the levelling-out lawn ahead tricked the ground estimate, and the robot stopped for grass. That was already true before this work (it's slightly better now), and it's the first job for the next step: slopes.

docs.title: The long-grass rule, and three ways to trap a robot in a patch of grass
docs.text:
Last night's result was uncomfortable: the 3D lidar sees a 10 cm hedgehog in 5 cm grass and loses it in 7 cm grass. Height is all the lidar measures, so the lawn has to stay short enough for an animal to stand out of it. That's the long-grass rule (decision D2): if the uncut grass ahead is too tall, the robot doesn't mow it. It stops the blade, goes home and says the lawn is overdue. An owner switch in the app turns the rule off for one mow.

Building it took one measurement that worked first time, one rule that worked first time, and a clearance that trapped the robot three different ways before we found the version that can't.

docs.title: Measuring grass with a lidar
docs.text:
The safety gate already knows the height of every return above the local ground (5.1). In the lane the blade is about to cut, 0.6 to 2.0 m ahead and 0.6 m wide, we take the tallest return in each 20 cm cell (that's the grass top there) and then the median over the cells. A hedgehog or a box fills a cell or two, so it moves the median by nothing. Returns over 30 cm (a pole, a wall) aren't grass and are dropped first.

Before trusting it we calibrated it on four lawns of known height, driving straight with nothing in the way:

Run Grass (nominal) Measured (median) cal-g4-none-3d 4 cm 4.1 cm cal-g6-none-3d 6 cm 5.9 cm cal-g8-none-3d 8 cm 8.0 cm cal-g10-none-3d 10 cm 9.9 cm

Within 2 mm. (The sim's tufts are nominal ±25%, and "tallest per cell" lands near the nominal because the lidar doesn't hit every tuft's tip.) The gate publishes it as /grass/height, a rolling median over about a second.

docs.title: The rule
docs.text:
long_grass.py, pure Python with its own tests: when /grass/height stays over the limit (long_grass_m, default 5.5 cm, still Chris's call under D2) for 2 s of mowing, the rule trips once:

  • the blade stops immediately;
  • the robot keeps following its line with the blade off until it's somewhere a pivot is safe, then goes home;
  • after docking, the mission ends mission_abort: lawn overdue: uncut grass 9.1 cm > 5.5 cm, and the light ring shows the fault.

The 2 s hold is so a single tall clump at a stripe end doesn't end a mission.

The test lawn is the Open patch at 4 cm, with a 9 cm patch in its far corner (GRASS_PATCH). make long-grass-test mows it twice and analysis/long_grass_report.py judges each run:

Run Check Result longgrass-6-refuse rule tripped 9.1 cm > 5.5 cm, 0.8 m before the patch blade off 0.01 s after the trip blade-on distance inside the patch 0.00 m went home, docked, "lawn overdue" yes

That half passed on its first real try. The very first attempt doesn't count: mow-run defaults to the 2D lidar, which measures no grass, so the robot happily mowed the long patch. The grass report said "Lidar: 2d" and we read it too late. make long-grass-test now sets the 3D lidar itself.

docs.title: The other half: mow it anyway
docs.text:
With the owner switch on, the robot should mow the long patch. But the gate's clearance was a fixed number set for 4 cm grass (8 cm), and 9 cm grass has tufts up to 11 cm, so the gate stops for the patch like it would for a wall. "Mow long grass" has to mean the clearance follows the grass. So grass_clearance_auto: clearance = measured grass × 1.25 + 3 cm (the 5.1 rule), never above a cap (grass_clearance_max_m, 10 cm by default, 16 cm with the switch on). Then it trapped the robot three times.

Trap 1, driving out of the patch (longgrass-switch-3). The measuring lane starts 0.6 m ahead. Leaving the patch, the lane reached short grass while 0.9 m of long grass was still in front of the nose. The clearance dropped to the short grass, the gate stopped for the long grass, and standing still the lane kept seeing short grass: deadlock. Fix attempt: keep a measurement until the robot has driven past it (an odometer in the gate).

Trap 2: the gate crashed (longgrass-switch-4). Not a grass problem. A STOP during a turn on the spot with nothing in the corridor ahead made the log line format None, and the safety gate died. With no gate nothing reaches the motors, so the robot stopped, but a safety node that can be crashed by its own log line is a bug. It had been there since the pivot circle went in last night; no earlier run had pivot-stopped with an empty corridor. Fixed, with a test.

Trap 3, pivoting in the patch (longgrass-switch-5). At a stripe end the turn swings the lane onto short grass, which (by the odometer rule) counts as travel, while the pivot circle around the robot is full of 9 cm grass. Fix attempt: measure grass where each field looks: a near lane and the pivot circle itself, not just far ahead.

Trap 4, pivoting beside the patch (longgrass-6-mow). Mowing the short grass along the patch's edge, the pivot circle caught a slice of it. Most of the circle is short grass, so its median said short, and the slice of long grass, by height alone, is an obstacle the shape of a slice.

Each fix was local and each trap was the same thing: long grass where the field looks, a measurement that looks somewhere else. So the last version doesn't try to be local. The clearance only goes up during a mission: it's the tallest grass measured so far, anywhere, capped. That can't deadlock. Grass the robot could pass before, it can pass again. And it isn't a loss of safety where it matters. With the rule on, the mission ends before the grass is over 5.5 cm, so the clearance never passes ~10 cm. With the switch on, the owner has accepted exactly this: in long grass the lidar can't see a hedgehog.

make long-grass-test LG_RUN=longgrass-7, both halves:

Run Check Result longgrass-7-refuse rule tripped, blade off, never inside the patch, docked, "lawn overdue" PASS (9.0 cm > 5.5 cm) longgrass-7-mow switch logged, rule never trips PASS blade-on distance inside the patch 22.9 m (needs ≥ 16.7 m) mission done, coverage 98.2% safety stops 0

Then the question that matters more than coverage: does an automatic clearance still see the hedgehog? The danger would be the hedgehog standing in the lane and raising the measured grass, so the clearance rises over it. The median should stop that, and it did:

Run Result lg-auto5-hedgehog-3d (5 cm grass, auto clearance) PASS: seen at 1.18 m, stopped with 0.57 m to spare lg-auto5-none-3d (same, no obstacle) PASS: no false stops lg-flat-hose-3d (flat lawn, default gate, regression) PASS: seen at 1.29 m, 0.57 m to spare

docs.title: What we learned
docs.text:
• Calibrate a measurement before you build on it. Four short runs turned "it probably reads the grass" into "within 2 mm".
  • A clearance that adapts must adapt where the field looks, or not go down. We tried the first twice and it kept finding new places where it didn't. The ratchet is less clever and has no such places.
  • Height can't tell a strip of long grass from an object. Nothing in the lidar's geometry will fix that. It's why the plan has a camera (5.3).
  • Run every stop path, including the logging. The crash was in the line that explains a stop.

Not built: cutting the sim grass where the robot mows (tiles). The rule needs the uncut grass ahead, which the lane gives directly, and a thousand tile models would make the lidar render slower. Next: 5.1b, lidar health.

docs.title: Why Vector wandered: friction with no favourite
docs.text: Last time, Vector was the one platform still failing its smoke test. It ran 16 to 18 cm off its path (the limit is 15), and its heading estimate was off by about 3° (the limit is 2°). We blamed its filter. The filter was fine: the simulated tyres weren't.

docs.title: The clue: it never turned about its middle
docs.text:
A skid-steer like Vector turns in place by running its left wheels forward and its right wheels back. It should spin about the middle of its wheelbase, which is where its centre is in the plan. So we measured how far its centre actually moved during every turn in place of more than 20° (scripts/pivot_probe.py):

Platform Centre moved per turn in place (median) Worst Ion (2 wheels + caster) 0.6 cm 2.8 cm Tachyon (2 wheels + 2 casters) 1.0 cm 3.8 cm Graviton (tracks, 3 road wheels a side) 3.2 cm 7.4 cm Vector (4 wheels, 2 axles) 20 cm 29 cm

From the smoke-9 runs, ground truth.

Vector wasn't spinning about its middle. It spun about whichever axle happened to grip, and could change its mind part-way through a turn. The axles are 48 cm apart, so turning about one of them throws the centre sideways by up to 24 cm per turn. Every stripe end began with the robot well off its line, and every RTK fix that pulled the estimate back also bent the heading.

docs.title: Why: plain friction has no favourite
docs.text:
The simulator models each tyre's grip as plain friction: it resists sliding with the same force at any sliding speed. Now picture Vector turning in place. The tyres on whichever axle is further from the turning point slide sideways faster. But with two axles, the two sliding speeds always add up to the same total, wherever between the axles the turning point is:

  • about the middle, each axle slides at 24 cm per radian of turn: 24 + 24 = 48;
  • about the front axle, the front doesn't slide and the rear slides at 48: 0 + 48 = 48.

Same sliding, same force, same energy lost: the simulator had no reason to prefer the middle, so any small nudge moved the turning point. With three wheels a side, Graviton's middle road wheel breaks the tie (about the middle: r + 0 + r; about the front: 0 + r + 2r), which is why it only wandered 3 cm.

A real tyre isn't like that. Its sideways grip builds up with how fast it slips sideways, so sliding twice as fast on one axle costs more than sliding at half speed on both. That makes the middle the one cheapest turning point, which is why real skid-steer robots turn about their middle.

docs.title: The fix: give the tyres side-slip
docs.text:
Gazebo has a model for exactly this: tyre slip compliance, where sideways force grows with sideways slip. Vector's four wheels now have it (WheelSlip, lateral compliance 1.0). Two things then needed re-tuning:

  • Turns fell a third short. Tyres that give sideways resist turning more, so the same wheel speeds turned Vector only 0.67 as fast as its odometry expected. Its scrub factor (how much wider the wheels act than they are, when turning) went from 1.4 to 2.1. The turn calibration is back to 1.01. Field studies of skid-steer robots report factors of 1.5 to 2.5, so 2.1 is believable.
  • Docking. At docking speed (0.15 m/s), a skid-steer with real tyre side-slip barely turns while rolling: told to turn at 0.07 rad/s, it turned at 0.005. When its last turn in place onto the dock line finished 6° off, it couldn't steer that out. It reached the contacts 4 cm to one side three times running and gave up. The final line-up now finishes within 2.3° instead of 5.7°, for every platform.

Vector's longer path-following lookahead (0.9 m, set last time to stop a weave) wasn't needed any more: the weave was the old friction too. It's back to Ion's 0.5 m. Two small steering fixes from the hunt stayed, for every robot: the aim point never gets closer than 25 cm, even just before a corner, and the start of a path counts as a corner (a leg that starts more than 17° off begins with a turn in place).

We first gave the tracks side-slip too, and Graviton started wobbling along its stripes (it covered 95.3% instead of 99.2%). Tracks didn't need it, so they don't get it. A test now checks that only two-axle skid-steer has it.
