Vector's took the second try in both of its last two runs, so its docking is the weakest part left. The Platforms page battle cards show these results.

docs.title: What this doesn't prove
docs.text: The side-slip setting is a modelling choice, not a measurement: the right value depends on the tyres and the grass. It's the difference between a simulator that can't pick a turning point and one that turns about the middle, as real skid-steers do. The scrub factor (2.1) and the docking line-up will need checking on a real Vector. A real skid-steer at walking pace also needs a firm push to turn at all, and the simulator now shows that too. Docking is where that matters most, so it's the first thing to watch on real hardware.

docs.title: Too steep
docs.text: The second ground hazard after drop-offs: a slope too steep to drive up, or to drive across without sliding. This post gives the robot a slope limit, two ways to see a steep bank coming, and a backstop for when it doesn't.

docs.title: How steep is too steep?
docs.text:
The limit comes from the robot itself, not from a number typed into the code. Ion is modelled on a YardForce Classic 500, which the maker rates for slopes up to 30% (16.7°). Ion's own limit is 15°, a little inside that.

Driving across a slope is different. A low mower like this won't tip over until about 55°, but on wet grass its tyres start to slide sideways at about 19°. So the sideways limit is a bit lower: 90% of the climb limit, 13.5° for Ion. From 80% of either limit the robot slows down.

Those numbers are defaults for Chris to check on the real lawn. The first two guesses were too strict, as it turned out (more below).

docs.title: A plateau with a steep side
docs.text:
The simulated yard got a new patch: a 20 cm plateau with a bank on its west side. The south half of the bank is a gentle 7°, the north half a steep 20°, and the plateau's south side ends in a wall.

The map layer. On the correct map, the steep half of the bank is marked as a keep-out, and the robot keeps the same extra margin from it as from a raised flowerbed. It mowed 97.7% of the patch it could reach and finished normally. It never tilted more than 7° and never came closer than 35 cm to the wall's edge.

The sensing layer is for a map that doesn't know about the bank. The robot has three checks:

  • Up or down, ahead. It fits a line to the ground 0.5 to 2 m past its nose and adds its own pitch. A run of ground only counts if it's a clean line, so a box or a flowerbed isn't mistaken for a ramp.
  • Sideways, ahead. It measures the ground under where each wheel is about to go, and the difference between the two sides over a metre, plus its own roll.
  • The backstop. The robot's own tilt sensor, averaged over a second. If it is ever tilted past a limit, it stops.

Over a limit, it does what it does at a drop: it stops, backs straight out by 30 cm, and gives up the mission with the reason, so a person can look.

With the bank left off the map, the robot saw it while the steep part was still 1.1 m past its nose, stopped, backed off and gave up. It never tilted more than 5° sideways and never entered the bank.

docs.title: What broke on the way
docs.text:
• The bank was beside the robot, not ahead of it. The first unmapped run planned its outer lap along the foot of the steep bank. Looking ahead, the ground was flat, so the up/down check saw nothing. One wheel climbed the bank until the tilt backstop stopped it at 12.7° of roll, well inside the bank. That's what the sideways check is for.
  • The lowest point is in the wrong place. The first sideways check used the lowest laser return in each 20 cm patch of ground. On a sideways slope that is always the patch's downhill edge, so a 20° bank read as 4°. The check now looks at narrow strips right under each wheel track instead.
  • The top of a ramp looked like a step. Where a ramp levels out, the ground estimate changed so abruptly that it was thrown away, and the ramp's top read as an obstacle. A ground estimate that drops away is now kept when it clearly matches the ground just ahead.
  • The limits were too strict for a lumpy lawn. The bumpy test lawn is an ordinary 25 cm mound with small bumps on it. Across it, the robot rolls 10° even averaged over a second, and a diagonal across the mound's flank really tips 12.4° over a metre. With a sideways limit of 10°, then 12°, the robot refused to mow it. An offline check of the sideways measurement against the true terrain showed it's accurate: on average it's off by 0.04°, and a single reading by at most 2.8°. The limit was the problem, not the measurement. It's now 13.5°, and one stray reading isn't enough: the slope has to be seen in three scans in a row.
  • A hilltop looked like a cliff. Climbing the bumpy lawn's mound at about 6°, the robot is tipped back, so in its own frame the ground 2 m ahead sits about 21 cm lower than it really is. At the top, the far side read as a 20 cm drop, and the robot gave up mowing a perfectly ordinary lawn. The drop check now measures heights along gravity, levelling the lidar's picture with the tilt sensor first. Replayed at the same spots: 4 false drops before, none after, and the terrace's real walls are still seen.
  • The route home went straight down the bank. With the extra margin around the tree, the wall and the steep bank, the plateau had no way out that kept every margin. When the route planner found no route, it fell back to a straight line, and that line ran down the mapped 20° bank. The robot stopped at its foot. Now the route home tries again without the extra margin, still keeping clear of every keep-out, and if there's still no way, it stops and asks for help rather than drive through a keep-out.

docs.title: Did it break anything?
docs.text:
• The bumpy lawn (7 cm grass) mowed 97% and finished, with no false drop at the hilltop any more. But it made one false stop for grass, climbing the foot of the mound. That's 2.8 false stops per 100 m², over our bar of 1. It isn't new: the ground estimate still struggles where a slope begins or ends under grass, and it's the next ground-estimate job.
  • The terrace with the wrong map still stops for the real wall and gives up. The closest the robot's front corner came to the edge was 9 cm (12 cm last time). That's the same weak spot as before: a turn that swings the robot toward an edge brings it into view late.
  • The obstacle course still passes: every obstacle on bare ground, and everything but the hose in 7 cm grass.

docs.title: Not covered yet
docs.text:
• Wheel slip. A wet slope the robot can't climb shows up as wheels turning while the robot doesn't move. The satellite fix can see that; it's not built yet.
  • The real limits. 15° up, 13.5° across and slowing at 80% are defaults until they're checked on Chris's lawn.
  • Next: is the lidar telling the truth? Everything above trusts the lidar. The next step checks it: a dirty or wet window, rain, a frozen or silent sensor. Its first test run already found something: 7 cm grass looked like rain to it.

docs.title: Build manual
docs.text:
The goal: someone who isn't us can buy the parts, build a robot, and prove it is safe and working, with the same pass/fail style as the simulator reports in the devlog.

This is a hobby project, not a certified product

You are responsible for whatever you build. Until the blade-on checklist passes, the blade stays off the motor. A robot that drives the lawn without cutting is still a complete localization and navigation project.

docs.title: How this manual is organised
docs.text:
It follows the four kinds of documentation (tutorials, how-to guides, reference, explanation), because a first build, a blade swap and a torque value are different jobs and need different pages.

Kind You want to… Pages Tutorial build your first robot, start to finish H1: bench and push-cart · H2: brain transplant · H3: blade on (H2 and H3 are drafts until the hardware arrives) How-to do one job Buy the parts · Check parts on arrival Reference look something up End-of-line test · Verification and acceptance tests · Build record and quality Explanation know why the devlog: every design decision has a post

docs.title: The rules every page follows
docs.text:
1. One action per step, with the tools it needs and roughly how long it takes.
  2. Safety notes are red boxes, inline, before the step they apply to: never in an appendix.
  3. Every sub-assembly ends at a checkpoint: a short test with a pass/fail result. Fail = stop. Don't build on top of a failed checkpoint; use the troubleshooting notes on that page.
  4. Every checkpoint is recorded in the robot's build record, so a robot's history can be traced from its serial number.
  5. Verification uses the simulator's reports, run on the real robot with the same thresholds (or documented, looser ones). If the sim says "localization within 5 cm RMS", the real robot has to show it too.

docs.title: The build stages
docs.text: Stage What you have at the end Blade H1 Bench and push-cart Pi 5 + RTK GNSS + IMU on a garden cart; a surveyed lawn boundary none H2 Brain transplant A used robot mower chassis driven by our software, docking and charging disconnected and taped H3 Blade on Supervised mowing after the safety gate passes on, after gate 3 H4 Custom chassis Our own frame, motors and battery (optional, later) on

docs.title: Build record and quality
docs.text: Every robot gets a serial number and a build record: a JSON file that says what went into it, which checkpoints it passed, and its calibration. It is telemetry like any run: indexed in Elasticsearch, so "which robots have fuse lot 2311?" is one query.

docs.title: The build record
docs.text:
{
  "serial": "MB-0001",
  "revisions": {"bom": "H2-r1", "pcb": "carrier-v1.2.0", "software": "git:08d9263"},
  "parts": [
    {"bom_row": 3, "part": "ZED-F9P board", "supplier": "…", "order": "…", "lot": "…", "receiving": "pass"},
    {"bom_row": 0, "part": "STOP button", "lot": "…", "receiving": "pass"}
  ],
  "checkpoints": [
    {"id": "H1-C", "result": "pass", "measured": {"fix_s": 74, "scatter_95_cm": 1.8}, "by": "…", "at": "2026-…"}
  ],
  "calibration": {"antenna_xyz_m": [0.0, 0.0, 0.42], "imu_rpy_deg": [0.3, -0.5, 0.0]},
  "acceptance": [{"gate": 2, "run_id": "…", "report": "coverage", "result": "pass"}]
}

A robot ships (or goes on the lawn unattended) only when every checkpoint and every gate passed on its current revisions. Changing a safety-chain part, the PCB revision, or the software that runs the safety gate means re-running gate 3.

docs.title: Quality controls
docs.text:
Control What When Receiving inspection The checks on arrival; safety-chain parts: every part. Other parts: a sample of each lot Every delivery First-article inspection The first robot of a new BOM or PCB revision goes through every checkpoint and every gate, with photos Each new revision Checkpoints The pass/fail tests at the end of each sub-assembly Every robot End-of-line test One script on the finished robot: every sensor and actuator, the STOP and blade stop times, the watchdog Every robot Defect log Every failed checkpoint, field return and safety event: what, which serial, which lots, the cause, the fix Always Revision control BOM and PCB revisions are in the repository and on the build record; no unrecorded changes Always

Build records live in the repository as build-records/<serial>.json, so every change to one is a commit.

make build-record-eol SERIAL=MB-0001 RUN_ID=<run>   # add an end-of-line result, stamped with the current revisions
make builds                                          # validate every record, index them into Elasticsearch, print status

make builds prints what each robot is allowed to do on its current revisions: drive blade-off needs a clean record and an end-of-line PASS; supervised mowing also needs gates 2 and 3. A result on an older software, PCB or BOM revision is history, not evidence, so changing a revision silently withdraws those permissions until the tests are rerun. In Elasticsearch, fauerbot-builds has one document per robot and fauerbot-build-parts one per part: "which robots have fuse lot 2311?" is a term query on lot.

docs.title: End-of-line test
docs.text:
One script, run on the finished robot, that checks every sensor, every actuator and the safety chain, then writes a pass/fail report and the end_of_line entry for the robot's build record. It's the last thing that happens to a robot before it's called built, and the first thing to rerun after a repair.

It uses only the robot's own sensors: wheel encoders, IMU, GNSS, lidar, battery. Nothing comes from the simulator's ground truth, so the script that passes in the simulator is the same script you run on the real robot.

make eol-run                      # in the simulator (a box is placed 3.5 m ahead for step 6)
make eol-run SERIAL=MB-0001       # the serial goes in the report and the build-record entry

On the robot: ros2 run fauerbot_safety eol_test --ros-args -p serial:=MB-0001 -p blade:=false -p lidar:=false (H2: blade disconnected, no lidar yet; those rows report SKIP).

Before you run it on a real robot

  • About 4 m of clear, flat lawn ahead, nobody within 3 m, and a box (at least 20 cm tall) about 3 m in front of the robot.
  • The test drives the robot and, unless blade:=false, spins the blade. Keep a hand near the STOP button for the whole run.
  • Until gate 3 passes: blade:=false, the blade off the motor and the connector taped.

docs.title: What it checks
docs.text:
Every command goes through the safety gate, exactly as a mowing mission's would, so the test exercises the whole chain and not just the motors.

Step What the test does Pass if 1 sensors Listens for 5 s with the robot still IMU, GNSS, joint states, lidar and battery at ≥ 90% of their rates; gravity 9.81 ± 0.3 m/s²; gyro bias ≤ 0.02 rad/s; RTK fixed with σ ≤ 5 cm; battery a sane 7S voltage and ≥ 30%; STOP not latched 2 wheels Forward at 0.2 m/s, pivot left, pivot right; then turns back to the start heading on the gyro Each wheel within 10% of the speed the command implies, with the right sign; IMU yaw rate matches within 15%. Catches a swapped motor, a reversed encoder, a wrongly mounted IMU 3 blade Spins up with the 3 s soft start, then commands it off 90% speed within 4 s; below 10% within 2 s 4 STOP Drives at 0.3 m/s with the blade on and presses STOP while the driver keeps commanding motion Standstill ≤ 1 s; blade below 10% ≤ 2 s; nothing moves for 3 s while latched; ring red; release (GO held 2 s) leaves it stopped 5 watchdog Drives with the blade on, then the driver goes silent Drive stops ≤ 1 s; blade below 10% ≤ 3 s 6 obstacle Drives at the box and keeps asking to drive on The safety gate stops it, ≥ 10 cm from the box 7 manual Lists what a script can't do Lift, tilt, bumper, unplugging each interlock connector, hanging the microcontroller: an operator does these from gate 3 (hardware/safety.md) and signs each one on the build record

The blade-stop limit (2 s) is our target, not a measured number: gate 3 measures the real motor's stop time and the limit is set from that, in writing, never quietly in code.

docs.title: What it found in the simulator
docs.text:
The first run (eol-1) passed everything except the watchdog. When the driver went silent the robot simply carried on: Gazebo's drive plugin, like many real motor controllers, keeps executing the last command it got. Nothing in our software timed commands out. Now the safety gate does: a driver that wants motion has to keep saying so, every 0.5 s or less, or the gate sends zero.

The second run (eol-2) found something else: each time the blade was cut, the whole robot twisted by about 8°. The simulated blade motor had unlimited torque and stopped the blade within one 1 ms physics step; the reaction twisted the chassis. After STOP and the watchdog the robot pointed 16° off and drove past the box. The simulated motor is now torque-limited (±3 N·m), and the blade stops in 0.75 s, a believable number to test against.

Run Watchdog: drive stops Blade stop (commanded) Twist from the blade stops (ground truth) Result eol-1 never 0.01 s 8° (one stop; the watchdog never cut the blade) FAIL eol-2 (watchdog) 0.51 s 0.01 s 8° + 8° FAIL (missed the box) eol-3 (torque-limited blade) 0.54 s 0.75 s < 0.1° PASS

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
• reports/<run_id>-eol.md: the table above, with every measured value.
  • reports/<run_id>-eol.json: the end_of_line block of the build record (serial, run id, time, every check's result and measurement).
  • The recorded bag (data/runs/<run_id>) and the eol_check telemetry events in Elasticsearch, like every run.

docs.title: H1: bench and push-cart
docs.text:
What you build: a Raspberry Pi 5 with RTK GNSS and an IMU, strapped to a garden cart. You push it round your lawn and it records the boundary to a few centimetres. That boundary becomes the lawn file the mowing planner uses.

Time: two weekends. Cost: see hardware/bom.md, stage H1. Blade: none at this stage.

Tools: a laptop with Docker; a multimeter; small screwdrivers; cable ties; a tape measure; for step 6, a tripod or a fixed post.

Safety for this stage

  • Only the Pi's own USB-C supply or a USB power bank powers this stage: no lithium pack wiring yet.
  • Unplug the power before connecting or disconnecting anything (GNSS, IMU, antenna).
  • Mount the antenna where a falling cart can't drive the mast into someone; keep the cable away from wheels.

docs.title: 1. Put the Pi together (20 min)
docs.text: Fit the active cooler, then the NVMe HAT and SSD. Don't power it yet.

docs.title: 2. Flash and boot (30 min)
docs.text:
Flash Ubuntu 24.04 server (arm64) to the SSD with Raspberry Pi Imager. Enable SSH and set a strong password in the imager. Boot it.

Checkpoint H1-A: the Pi

vcgencmd get_throttled returns 0x0 after 10 minutes idle, and the CPU temperature (vcgencmd measure_temp) stays below 70 °C. Fail: check the PSU (it must be the 27 W one) and the cooler's connector.

docs.title: 3. Install Docker and the robot's container (40 min)
docs.text:
Install Docker from Docker's own apt repository, clone the repository, and run make test. It's the same container image as the simulator, built for arm64: what passes on the laptop must pass here.

Checkpoint H1-B: same software

make test passes on the Pi with the same test count as on the laptop.

docs.title: 4. Connect the GNSS receiver (20 min)
docs.text: Power off. Screw the antenna cable to the ZED-F9P board before powering it, then connect the board by USB. Power on and check that /dev/ttyACM0 (or similar) appears.

docs.title: 5. Configure corrections (30 min)
docs.text: Set up the NTRIP client with your corrections source: a state CORS network or your own base station (BOM row 6/7). Never commit the caster password to the repository; it goes in a local .env file.

docs.title: 6. Static test (15 min + 10 min logging)
docs.text:
Put the antenna on a tripod or post with a clear view of the sky, away from walls and trees. Log 10 minutes.

Checkpoint H1-C: RTK fix

RTK FIXED within 5 minutes of a cold start; over 10 minutes, the horizontal scatter is within ±3 cm (95% of samples). Fail: check the antenna has a clear sky view and a ground plane, the corrections are arriving (NTRIP client log), and the antenna is multiband. Judge it with make gnss-static-report RUN_ID=h1-c BAG=<the bag>: the same script the simulator passes.

docs.title: 7. Connect the IMU (20 min)
docs.text:
Power off. Connect the BNO085 to the Pi's I²C pins with the STEMMA QT cable (3.3 V, never 5 V). Power on.

Checkpoint H1-D: IMU

i2cdetect -y 1 shows the IMU at 0x4A or 0x4B. Rotate the board 90° on a flat table: the heading changes by 90° ± 3°. Tilt it by about 20°: roll or pitch shows it, and the sign matches the robot's axis convention (x forward, y left, z up).

docs.title: 8. Mount everything on the cart (45 min)
docs.text:
Antenna at the highest point, on the cart's centreline, with its position measured from the axle (x, y, z in metres): those numbers go in the robot description, exactly like the sim robot's. IMU flat and fixed rigidly (a wobbling IMU reads the wobble). Pi and power bank in a box, out of the rain.

Checkpoint H1-E: mounting

Antenna and IMU offsets measured and written into the build record. The IMU reads level (roll and pitch within 2°) with the cart on flat ground.

docs.title: 9. Survey the lawn (30 min per lawn)
docs.text:
Walk the boundary slowly with RTK FIXED, then each flowerbed and tree as a keep-out. Record a bag.

Checkpoint H1-F: the survey

The boundary closes on itself within 5 cm. The polygon, drawn over a satellite image, matches the lawn edge. Commit it as the lawn file (GeoJSON, like config/lawns/sim-yard.geojson); the same planner as in the sim plans it.

Stage H1 done: record the checkpoint results in the build record; next is verification gate 1.

docs.title: H2: brain transplant, blade off
docs.text:
What you build: a used robot mower whose own electronics are replaced by the OpenMower mainboard, driven by our software: the H1 Pi, GNSS and IMU move inside. At the end it mows your lawn's pattern without cutting, returns to its dock and charges.

Time: about three weekends. Cost: hardware/bom.md, stage H2. Blade: removed from the motor, the connector taped, for the whole of this stage.

Draft: written before the hardware arrived

The steps follow hardware/build-guide.md and our own checkpoints; the times are estimates. The mainboard itself is fitted by OpenMower's own step-by-step guide, not by this page: it's specific to your mower's revision and theirs is the authority. This page will be rewritten from the real build, with photos.

Tools: everything from H1; Torx and Phillips drivers (the mower's screws); cut-resistant gloves; a multimeter; insulating tape; a sturdy box to stand the robot on with its wheels off the ground.

Safety for this stage

  • Disconnect the mower's battery before opening the body, and before connecting or disconnecting anything inside. The pack is a lithium pack: don't puncture, crush or short it, and keep it away from metal tools.
  • Wear cut-resistant gloves whenever you touch the blade, even a blunt one.
  • The blade comes off in step 3 and stays off until H3. Driving tests are done blade-off because a software bug at this stage should cost a flowerbed, not a foot.
  • Wheels-off-the-ground tests first: a robot on a box can't drive into anyone.

docs.title: 1. Choose and check the mower (before buying)
docs.text:
Check the mower's model and revision against the OpenMower compatibility list before you pay for it, and that the mainboard kit version matches it (hardware/bom.md, rows 10–11).

Checkpoint H2-A: the stock mower works

With its own firmware, the mower drives, mows, finds its dock and charges. Record the battery voltage when it's full. Fail: don't convert a mower whose motors, battery or dock are already faulty; you'd never know which half is broken.

docs.title: 2. Open the body (30 min)
docs.text: Battery disconnected (see the safety box). Follow OpenMower's guide for your mower to remove the top cover. Photograph every connector before you unplug it.

docs.title: 3. Remove the blade (10 min)
docs.text:
Gloves on. Remove the blade from the motor, bag it and label it with the robot's serial. Tape the blade motor's connector (step 4 disconnects it from the board).

Checkpoint H2-B: no blade

Blade off, in its bag; the blade motor connector taped and unplugged. A photo of both goes in the build record.

docs.title: 4. Fit the mainboard (one afternoon)
docs.text: Follow OpenMower's step-by-step guide for your mower revision. Keep the mower's own stop button, lift and tilt sensors connected: they become inputs to the mainboard's emergency-stop chain, which is the hardware layer under our software.

docs.title: 5. First power-up, wheels off the ground (20 min)
docs.text:
Robot on the box, wheels free. Reconnect the battery. Power on.

Checkpoint H2-C: nothing moves by itself

At power-up no wheel turns. Pressing the stop button and lifting the body both show as emergency-stop in the mainboard's status. Fail: power off, battery out, and recheck the wiring against your photos.

docs.title: 6. Move the H1 electronics in (one afternoon)
docs.text:
Pi, GNSS board and IMU inside; the GNSS antenna on top, as high as the body allows, on the centreline. Measure the antenna's and the IMU's position from the middle of the rear axle (x forward, y left, z up, in metres): those numbers go into the robot description, as they did for the cart.

Checkpoint H2-D: offsets

Antenna and IMU offsets in the build record. With the robot on flat ground, the IMU reads level (roll and pitch within 2°) and RTK reaches FIXED within 5 minutes.

docs.title: 7. Connect our software to the mainboard (one weekend)
docs.text:
Bring up the ROS 2 bridge to the mainboard (OpenMowerNext is the ROS 2 Jazzy reference). The robot needs the same topics as the simulator: /cmd_vel, /joint_states (wheel speeds), /imu, /gps/fix, /battery, and the buttons on /ui/buttons. Then start the safety gate and the UI nodes, exactly as in the sim.

Checkpoint H2-E: the end-of-line test, wheels in the air

Still on the box: run the end-of-line test with blade:=false lidar:=false. Every wheel turns the right way at the right speed, STOP stops it, and the watchdog stops it when the driver goes silent. The three IMU yaw-rate rows fail in the air (the body isn't turning); that's expected here, and only here. Everything else must pass.

docs.title: 8. On the lawn (1 hour)
docs.text:
On the lawn, with the dock placed and its position surveyed with RTK, run the whole end-of-line test (blade:=false lidar:=false) and record the result in the build record.

Checkpoint H2-F: end-of-line PASS

Every automatic row PASS or SKIP (blade, lidar). Fail: don't go on to gate 2; the report says which row.

Stage H2 done: next is verification gate 2: drive, localize, mow the pattern (blade off), dock 10 times out of 10.

docs.title: H3: blade on
docs.text:
What you do: put the blade back on and prove, one recorded test at a time, that every way of stopping it works, before the robot cuts grass, first under supervision and only much later on its own.

Time: a weekend for the tests, then ten supervised mowing sessions. Blade: on, from step 3.

Draft: written before the hardware arrived

The order and the pass criteria are fixed (they're gate 3); how each test is physically done will be rewritten from the real robot, with photos.

Before you start

  • Gate 2 has passed on this robot's current revisions, and the defect log has no open safety item. If not, stop here.
  • Nobody within 5 m of the robot while the blade can turn, except the operator at the STOP button. No children or pets in the garden at all.
  • Cut-resistant gloves and the battery disconnected whenever a hand goes near the blade.
  • Eye protection and long trousers for every blade-on test: a blade throws stones.
  • Any failed test: disconnect the blade motor, tape the connector, log it. "Passed on the second try" is a fail.

docs.title: 1. Refit the blade (15 min)
docs.text: Battery disconnected, gloves on. Fit the blade from its labelled bag with the mower maker's screws and torque; check it turns freely by hand and doesn't touch the guard. Reconnect the blade motor connector.

docs.title: 2. Measure the blade stop time (30 min)
docs.text:
Robot on the lawn (the blade cuts air, not grass, for this). Spin the blade up through our software, press STOP, and record the blade speed from the motor controller's own speed reading until it stops. Repeat 5 times.

Checkpoint H3-A: the stop time

Five measured stop times in the build record; the worst one is the robot's blade stop time. It must be within the end-of-line limit (2 s target). Every later test uses this number.

docs.title: 3. End-of-line test, blade on (15 min)
docs.text:
Run the full end-of-line test with blade:=true (and lidar:=true once the lidar is fitted).

Checkpoint H3-B: end-of-line PASS with the blade

Every automatic row PASS, including the blade rows, the STOP blade-stop and the watchdog blade-stop.

docs.title: 4. The checks a script can't do (an afternoon)
docs.text:
Each one with the blade spinning, recorded as a run, the result signed on the build record. They're the 7 manual rows of the end-of-line report.

Test How Pass if Lift either side Lift the front, then each side, with a hook or strap, never by hand near the deck Blade below 10% within the measured stop time; it doesn't restart when put down Tilt Tilt the robot past the limit on a ramp Blade stops Bumper Push the body against a fixed post Drive and blade stop Interlock connectors Blade off, battery out: unplug one interlock connector. Battery in, ask for the blade The blade never starts. Repeat for each connector Hang the microcontroller The debug command that stops the firmware's main loop Blade stops (hardware watchdog) Kill the ROS software docker stop the robot's container while mowing Blade and drive stop RTK lost Cover the antenna while mowing near the boundary It stops inside the geofence margin

docs.title: 5. Supervised mowing (10 sessions)
docs.text:
Mow the lawn ten times with the operator watching and the STOP button in reach; each run's coverage, power and safety reports go in the build record.

Checkpoint H3-C: ten clean runs

Ten runs, no safety event, every report PASS. Only then can any unattended mowing even be considered, and the Phase 5 perception work (seeing people, pets and hedgehogs) comes first.

Stage H3 done: the robot is built. Any change to a safety-chain part, the PCB or the safety software means steps 2–4 again (build record).

docs.title: Buy the parts
docs.text: The bill of materials, with prices, sources and the date each price was checked, lives in the repository at hardware/bom.md. This page is the how: what to check before you order, what you can substitute and what you must not.

docs.title: Before you order: checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Read the whole stage first (for example the H1 tutorial), so you know what each part is for.
  • [ ] Re-check prices and stock. Every price in the BOM has a "checked on" date; anything older than 3 months is a guess. Single-board computer prices rose several times in 2025–2026.
  • [ ] Check lead times. RTK GNSS boards and genuine modules can be weeks out; order those first.
  • [ ] For H2: check the mower's revision against the OpenMower compatibility list before buying a used mower or a mainboard. The wrong carrier-board revision does not fit.
  • [ ] Region: chargers and the dock supply must match your mains (US 120 V / EU 230 V); check the plug and the rating on the label, not the listing.
  • [ ] Buy batteries only as complete packs with a BMS from a seller who ships them legally (UN38.3 paperwork). Don't build a pack.
  • [ ] Keep every receipt and order number: they go into the build record (part lots).

docs.title: What you can substitute
docs.text:
Part Substitute freely? Rule Raspberry Pi 5 (8 GB) With care 4 GB works for H1; the 8 GB leaves room for mapping and bags. Must be a Pi 5 (arm64, same container). NVMe SSD, cooler, PSU Yes Any reputable brand. The PSU must be the 27 W USB-C type (5 V 5 A); weaker supplies throttle the Pi. RTK GNSS receiver No: genuine u-blox ZED-F9P Clone or "compatible" F9P boards are common and fail RTK fix in ways that look like software bugs. Buy from the board maker or an authorised distributor. GNSS antenna Only multiband (L1/L2) A single-band antenna works but RTK takes far longer to fix and drops more often. IMU (BNO085) With care Another 9-DoF IMU needs its own driver and a new noise calibration; the sensor report must pass again. Fuses, fuse holders No Exactly the rating in the wiring drawing. A bigger fuse is not a safer fuse. STOP button, interlock relay / MOSFETs No Part of the safety chain: the exact part, or a re-run of every safety test at gate 3. Blade and blade bolts No The mower maker's genuine blades only. Never a sharpened replacement or a "universal" blade. Battery pack No (H2) / with care (H4) H2 uses the mower's own pack. H4: a 7S pack with BMS, about 150 Wh, from a reputable maker. Cable, connectors, heat-shrink Yes Same or larger wire gauge; never smaller.

Counterfeits

The parts most often faked are GNSS modules, IMUs, fuses and battery cells. If a price is far below every other seller's, assume it's a fake. The receiving inspection has the signs to look for.

docs.title: Ordering in batches (for more than one robot)
docs.text: Order safety-chain parts (STOP buttons, fuses, interlock parts) from one lot for a batch of robots, and record the lot number. If a lot turns out to be bad, the build record tells you exactly which robots have it.

docs.title: Check parts on arrival
docs.text: Do this the day the parts arrive, while you can still return them. Record the result (pass or fail and why) in the build record. A part that fails receiving inspection never goes into a robot.

docs.title: Every part
docs.text:
• [ ] The part number on the part matches the order and the BOM.
  • [ ] No transport damage: cracked housings, bent pins, crushed corners on the box.
  • [ ] Note the lot or batch number if there is one (photo of the label).

docs.title: Electronics
docs.text: Part Check Fail if ZED-F9P GNSS board The u-blox module's laser marking is sharp and the board maker's name is printed on the PCB; connect it over USB and read the firmware version Blurry or printed (not etched) marking; module reports an unknown or odd firmware Raspberry Pi 5 Boots from a known-good card; vcgencmd get_throttled reads 0x0 with the official PSU Doesn't boot; throttling with the official PSU IMU (BNO085) Detected on I²C at address 0x4A or 0x4B Not detected; wrong chip ID Fuses Rating printed on the fuse matches the wiring drawing; the body is the brand you ordered Missing or smudged rating; a different brand to the listing STOP button Pressing latches it; twisting releases it; contacts open when pressed (measure with a multimeter) Doesn't latch; contacts close instead of open (wrong type: must be normally closed)

docs.title: Batteries
docs.text:
Lithium batteries

Inspect batteries outdoors or on a non-flammable surface. Never charge a pack that is swollen, dented, warm, or smells sweet. Put it in a metal box outside and contact the seller.

  • [ ] No swelling: the pack sits flat and the case isn't bulging.
  • [ ] Open-circuit voltage is within the "storage" range for its chemistry (for a 7S Li-ion pack, about 25–27 V; the full range is 21–29.4 V). Below 21 V: don't charge it.
  • [ ] The connector matches the wiring drawing, and its polarity is right (measure; don't trust wire colours).
  • [ ] The BMS label and UN38.3 paperwork are present.

docs.title: Mechanical (H2: a used mower)
docs.text:
• [ ] Wheels turn freely by hand with the motors unplugged; no grinding.
  • [ ] The blade disc and guard are intact: no cracks, nothing bent.
  • [ ] The rain seals are present and not perished.
  • [ ] The dock's contacts are clean and springy.

docs.title: Verification and acceptance tests
docs.text:
Verification = the simulator's reports, run on the real robot. Every behaviour in the devlog was proven in the simulator with a script that reads a recorded run and prints PASS or FAIL. The same scripts, with the same thresholds, are the robot's acceptance tests. Where real hardware needs a looser limit, the limit is written here with the reason, never quietly changed in code.

On the real robot there is no simulator "ground truth"; RTK GNSS (2–3 cm) plays that role, so thresholds tighter than about 3 cm can't be checked outdoors. Those are marked bench.

docs.title: Gate 1: sensors (H1)
docs.text: Test Script Pass if GNSS static gnss_static_report RTK FIXED within 5 min of a cold start and ≥ 95% of the time after; ±3 cm per axis (95% of fixes) over ≥ 10 min IMU and odometry noise sensor_report Measured noise within 50% of the model's; heading drift ≤ 1° over the run (bench, on a turntable) Data rate sensor_report ≥ 90% of each sensor's nominal rate; pairs aligned within 11 ms

docs.title: Gate 2: driving, blade off (H2)
docs.text: Test Script Pass if Drive a square drive_report Speed within 5% on straights; path error ≤ 10 cm; closes within 30 cm Localization localization_report Error ≤ 5 cm RMS, never above 15 cm; yaw ≤ 2° RMS Mow a lawn (blade disconnected) coverage_report ≥ 95% of the reachable area covered; no keep-out incursions; cross-track ≤ 15 cm while mowing Energy power_report Never below 10% state of charge; returns to the dock on its own Docking power_report / dock events 10 out of 10 docks, retries allowed Obstacles obstacle_report Stops ≥ 10 cm from every obstacle on the course (boxes, a hose, a soft toy) Buttons ui_report STOP: standstill ≤ 1.0 s; no motion while latched; release leaves it paused; "go home" docks and waits for GO

docs.title: Gate 3: blade on
docs.text:
Only after gate 2 passes, and with the end-of-line test passing with the blade on. The steps are in H3: blade on. Every item is a recorded run, analysed by a script, and kept with the build record.

Test Pass if STOP button Blade and drive stop; blade stop time measured and recorded; blade does not restart on release Lift either side Blade stops within the measured stop time; no automatic restart Tilt past the limit Blade stops Kill the ROS software Blade stops (watchdog) Hang the microcontroller Blade stops (hardware watchdog) Unplug each interlock connector in turn Blade stops (fail-safe wiring) RTK fix lost The robot stops inside the geofence margin Bumper hit Drive and blade stop 10 supervised mowing runs No safety event. Only then any unattended mowing

If any gate-3 test fails

Disconnect the blade motor, tape the connector, and record the failure in the defect log. Don't retest until the cause is understood and fixed; a "passed on the second try" is a fail.
